body.html:
Almost everything in this region is supplied by one artery: the external carotid. Learn where it starts, where it ends and its eight branches, and the arterial half of the lecture is done.

The venous side runs the other way, and two names carry most of it: the facial vein in front and the retromandibular vein behind. They meet, split and recombine to feed the internal and external jugular veins.

title: From the aorta to the carotid bifurcation
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
• The aorta is the largest artery in the body, originates from the left ventricle and is divided into three parts.
  • Right common carotid: arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the sternoclavicular joint.
  • Left common carotid: arises directly from the arch of the aorta, behind the manubrium sterni.
  • In the neck each common carotid ascends in the carotid sheath and divides in the carotid triangle, at the upper border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, opposite the disc between C3 and C4, into the external and internal carotid arteries.

Superior thyroid artery

Arises from the front of the external carotid, below the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. At the thyroid gland it divides into four terminal branches: infrahyoid (infrahyoid muscles), superior laryngeal (structures within the upper larynx), cricothyroid (cricothyroid muscle) and glandular (superior aspect of the thyroid gland).

Lingual artery

The principal artery of the tongue. Arises anteromedially from the external carotid opposite the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid, between the superior thyroid and facial arteries, and is divided into three parts by the hyoglossus. Four main branches: suprahyoid (suprahyoid muscles), dorsal lingual (back of the tongue and throat), sublingual (sublingual gland) and deep lingual (body and tip of the tongue).

Facial artery

Arises in the carotid triangle at the level of the hyoid bone. It travels superiorly and obliquely, underneath the digastric and closely related to the posterior surface of the submandibular gland, which it can pass through. It then curves upward over the body of the mandible along the anterior border of the masseter, deep to the platysma, and takes a tortuous course toward the angle of the mouth.

WhereBranchesSupply
NeckAscending palatineSoft palate and palatine tonsils
NeckTonsillarPalatine tonsils
NeckSubmentalFloor of the mouth and sublingual gland
NeckGlandularSubmandibular gland

FaceLateral nasalExternal nose
FaceAngular (termination)External nose, lower eyelid, orbicularis oculi, lacrimal sac

Occipital artery

Arises in the carotid triangle from the posterior aspect of the external carotid about 2 cm from its origin. It passes backward and upward under cover of the posterior belly of digastric, crossing the internal carotid, internal jugular vein and the hypoglossal and accessory nerves, then ascends tortuously in the dense superficial fascia of the scalp. It supplies sternocleidomastoid, the posterior neck and deep back muscles, the posterior part of the auricle, the scalp and occipital muscles, and gives mastoid and meningeal branches to the dura mater.

Ascending pharyngeal artery

The smallest branch, arising posteriorly near the origin of the external carotid. It ascends to the base of the skull between the wall of the pharynx and the internal carotid. Three named branches: pharyngeal (pharynx, constrictors, stylopharyngeus, soft palate, tonsils and auditory tube), inferior tympanic (medial wall of the middle ear) and meningeal (dura mater and several cranial nerves). Its relations include the sympathetic trunk and the hypoglossal, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

Posterior auricular artery

Supplies the back of the auricle, the external ear, the middle ear and the muscles around the mastoid process. Branches: auricular (back of the pinna and extrinsic auricular muscles), stylomastoid (enters the stylomastoid foramen to supply the middle and inner ear and the facial nerve as it exits), occipital (sternocleidomastoid, digastric, stylohyoid) and posterior tympanic.

Superficial temporal artery

A terminal branch. It divides into two main branches: the frontal (anterior) branch, supplying the muscles and skin of the forehead and the front of the scalp and anastomosing with the supraorbital and frontal arteries, and the parietal (posterior) branch, supplying the skin and muscles over the temporal and parietal regions. Other notable branches: transverse facial, zygomatico-orbital, anterior auricular and middle temporal.

Maxillary artery

The larger terminal branch, arising behind and below the mandibular neck, in the substance of the parotid gland. It runs forward medial to the neck of the mandible and enters the pterygopalatine fossa. It supplies the upper and lower jaws, the muscles of mastication, the nose, the palate and the meninges inside the skull (through the middle meningeal artery, which enters the foramen spinosum). Conventionally divided into three parts by the lateral pterygoid: mandibular, pterygoid and pterygopalatine, with five branches from each part.

title: External carotid artery: course and relations
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
It lies anterior to the internal carotid and is the chief arterial supply to structures in the front of the neck and face, under cover of the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. It supplies the neck, face and scalp, and also the tongue and the maxilla.

Course. At its origin the artery lies in the carotid triangle, anteromedial to the internal carotid. It begins lateral to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of the C3 to C4 disc, then ascends in a gentle spiral: first slightly forward, then backward and a little laterally, passing between the mastoid tip and the mandibular angle, ending lateral to the internal carotid.

Termination. In the substance of the parotid gland, behind the neck of the mandible, dividing into the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.

RegionRelations
With the internal carotidAt first medial to it; as it ascends it passes backward and lateral. It is crossed by the posterior belly of digastric and by stylohyoid.
In the neckMedially: the wall of the pharynx and the internal carotid. The stylopharyngeus and styloglossus muscles, the glossopharyngeal nerve and the pharyngeal branch of the vagus pass between the external and internal carotid arteries.
On the faceAnterolaterally overlapped at its beginning by sternocleidomastoid; above this it is comparatively superficial, covered by skin and fascia. Crossed by the hypoglossal nerve, the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid. Within the parotid gland it is crossed by the facial nerve. The internal jugular vein lies first lateral, then posterior to it.

The face is divided into areas that drain to specific lymph node groups.

RegionPrimary nodes
Upper face: forehead, lateral part of the eyelids, conjunctivaPreauricular (superficial parotid) nodes, in front of the ear
Central and lateral face: cheeks, upper lip, lateral aspects of the noseSubmandibular nodes, under the jaw
Lower face: lower lip, chin, apex of the tongueSubmental nodes, under the chin

Onward flow. From these primary groups lymph flows to more central nodes in the neck, the deep and superficial cervical nodes, then to the supraclavicular nodes. From there it enters the large veins at the root of the neck through the jugular trunks, emptying into the thoracic duct on the left side or the right lymphatic duct on the right.

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
• The external carotid artery's course and relationships.
  • Its branches and their important anatomic landmarks.
  • The venous system: superficial and deep.
  • The lymphatic system: superficial and deep.

The venous drainage of the face is primarily via the facial vein, which collects blood from the superficial structures of the face and drains into the internal jugular vein.

Superficial drainage

  • The supratrochlear and supraorbital veins merge at the medial angle of the eye to form the angular vein.
  • The angular vein becomes the facial vein as it descends the face, receiving tributaries that mirror the branches of the facial artery, including the superior and inferior labial veins.
  • It continues downward, passing over the masseter and superficial to the submandibular gland.
  • At the angle of the mandible it joins the anterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the common facial vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein, generally at the level of the hyoid bone.

Deep drainage and connections

  • The deep facial vein drains the buccal space and connects with the pterygoid venous plexus.
  • The pterygoid plexus has a crucial connection to the cavernous sinus, a potential pathway for infection to spread from the face to the brain. The facial vein is also connected to the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins.

Tributaries of the internal jugular vein: inferior petrosal sinus, facial vein, pharyngeal veins, lingual vein, superior thyroid vein and middle thyroid vein. It drains the brain (dural venous sinuses), face, thyroid gland and neck.

The brainstem is the stalk connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord, with the cerebellum hanging behind it. Three parts from top to bottom: midbrain, pons, medulla.

Two things carry the lecture: where each cranial nerve emerges, and the fact that the brainstem runs the vital functions, breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and consciousness.

Midbrain

The smallest part, about 2 cm, passing through the tentorial opening (foramen of Pacchioni). Two parts:

  • Tectum, behind the cerebral aqueduct: two superior and two inferior colliculi below the pineal gland. The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina (vision); the inferior brachium carries lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus fibres to the medial geniculate body (hearing). CN IV emerges below the colliculi.
  • Cerebral peduncles, paired and anterolateral, separated by the interpeduncular fossa. CN III exits between them; the optic tract runs round the top of the midbrain.

Pons

The largest part, from the metencephalon with the cerebellum. Its ventral bulge, about 2.5 cm, is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres. The basilar groove holds the basilar artery. The pontomedullary junction is a key landmark.

NerveEmerges at
CN V, trigeminalLateral mid-pons
CN VI, abducensPontomedullary junction, near the midline
CN VII, facialCerebellopontine angle
CN VIII, vestibulocochlearLateral to CN VII

Posterior surface, the floor of the fourth ventricle: the medial eminence in the midline; the facial colliculus, facial fibres looping round the abducens nucleus; and the stria medullaris marking the pons-medulla border. The cerebellopontine angle, where CN VII and VIII emerge beside the foramen of Luschka, lies at the junction of pons, medulla and cerebellum.

Medulla

The ventral median fissure, continuous with the cord's, is marked below by the decussation of 75 to 90 percent of corticospinal fibres. The pyramid on each side is made by the corticospinal tract; the olive lateral to it by the inferior olivary nucleus. CN XII emerges between pyramid and olive; CN IX, X and XI behind the olive.

As in the cord: white matter (descending motor and ascending sensory pathways), an ependymal cavity (the fourth ventricle and aqueduct of Sylvius) and grey matter (the cranial nerve nuclei and the reticular formation).

Reticular formation. Cell bodies and small axon bundles running in many directions, without distinct boundaries, spreading from the cord through the brainstem to the hypothalamus and thalamus. It integrates vital functions: arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation.

TractTypeCarries
Corticospinal and corticobulbarDescendingVoluntary movement of body and face
Dorsal column-medial lemniscusAscending, consciousTouch, proprioception, vibration
Anterolateral (spinothalamic)Ascending, consciousCrude touch, pain, temperature
SpinocerebellarAscending, unconsciousProprioception to the cerebellum

Fourth ventricle. Roof: the superior and inferior medullary vela. Floor: the rhomboid fossa. Side walls: the vela and cerebellar peduncles. The peak is the fastigium; the caudal tip the obex; widest at the pontomedullary junction. Choroid plexus lines the roof, and CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka.

The brainstem connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum. It lies in the posterior cranial fossa, on the clivus, under the tentorium cerebelli: above the cord, below the cerebrum and in front of the cerebellum. Ten of the twelve cranial nerves arise from its nuclei.

The growing neural tube bends at the cephalic flexure and the mesencephalic (cranial) flexure.

Connections. Above, the diencephalon by the transverse fissure of Bichat. Behind, the cerebellum by the cerebellar peduncles: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, inferior to the medulla. Below, the spinal cord through the foramen magnum.

Two rules. All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem except the optic and olfactory nerves. All emerge from the anterolateral surface except the trochlear nerve.

title: Blood supply, functions and clinical aspects
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
Blood supply: the basilar artery and its branches: the posterior cerebral artery and its peduncular branch, the superior cerebellar artery, the posterior choroidal artery and the interpeduncular branches.

Functions: a pathway for tracts between cortex and cord; the site of origin and emergence of CN III to XII; and the reticular formation, controlling consciousness, pain perception and cardiovascular and respiratory regulation.

Alternating syndrome. A peripheral cranial nerve lesion on one side with a hemiplegia on the other locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem.

Your professor's review questions: the thalamus is not part of the brainstem; the pyramids decussate in the medulla; the aqueduct passes through the midbrain; CN IV emerges dorsally; the respiratory and cardiovascular centres are in the medulla.

The cerebellum sits in the posterior cranial fossa, under the tentorium cerebelli and behind the pons and medulla, separated from them by the fourth ventricle. Three pairs of cerebellar peduncles tie it to the brainstem.

It does not start movements. It automatically regulates them: muscle tone, balance and the coordination of voluntary movement. It compares the movement you planned with the movement you are making and corrects the difference.

Remember one clinical rule above all: each cerebellar hemisphere controls the same side of the body, so cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion.

• Where the cerebellum lies and what surrounds it.
  • Its external configuration: vermis, hemispheres, surfaces, fissures and lobes.
  • The three cerebellar peduncles and what they carry.
  • Its internal configuration: cortex (three layers), deep nuclei, white matter (arbor vitae) and afferent fibres.
  • Its blood supply.
  • The three functional divisions and what happens when each is damaged.

Grayish-pink, in the posterior cranial fossa behind the brainstem.

DirectionRelations
SuperiorTentorium cerebelli, with the straight sinus in its midline and the great cerebral vein of Galen; the occipital lobe above the tentorium
AnteriorBrainstem and fourth ventricle; the lower end of the cerebral aqueduct and the quadrigeminal bodies
InferiorForamen magnum and the cisterns; sigmoid sinuses
Posterior and lateralOccipital bone and its dura; occipital sinus (if present) and the confluence of sinuses

Two cerebellar hemispheres joined in the midline by the vermis. The vermis controls axial muscles, posture and gait; the hemispheres coordinate limb movement. The surface is folded into thin transverse folia, giving a laminated look.

  • Superior surface: convex, under the tentorium.
  • Inferior surface: fits the posterior fossa; the vallecula, a deep median groove, houses the brainstem.
  • Cerebellar tonsils: rounded parts of the medial inferior hemispheres on each side of the inferior vermis, just above the foramen magnum.

Fissures (first, second and third order sulci):

  • Primary fissure: separates the smaller anterior lobe from the larger posterior lobe.
  • Posterolateral fissure: separates the posterior lobe from the flocculonodular lobe.
  • Great circumferential (horizontal) sulcus of Vicq d'Azyr: the most important landmark, separating the superior and inferior surfaces.

Three lobes: anterior, posterior and flocculonodular. The flocculonodular lobe is the oldest part (archicerebellum), connected with the vestibular nuclei, and serves balance and spatial orientation.

PeduncleJoins the cerebellum toMainly carries
Superior (brachium conjunctivum)MidbrainOutput: to the red nucleus and the thalamus (then motor cortex). Fine motor control, motor learning.
Middle (brachium pontis)PonsInput, the largest: pontocerebellar fibres from the contralateral pontine nuclei, bringing the motor plan from the cortex.
Inferior (restiform body)Medulla oblongataInput and output: spinocerebellar (proprioceptive) input; output to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation. Balance and posture.

Memory aid: Superior = Sends out; Middle = Massive input from the pons; Inferior = In and out.

On section, branching white matter surrounded by grey cortex makes the tree-like arbor vitae (tree of life).

Grey matter lies in two places: the folded cerebellar cortex on the surface and the four deep cerebellar nuclei in the white matter.

Cortex layer (outside in)Contents
MolecularInhibitory interneurons (stellate and basket cells), dendrites and parallel fibres
Purkinje cellA single row of large Purkinje cells: the only output of the cortex, and inhibitory, to the deep nuclei
GranularDensely packed granule cells and inhibitory Golgi cells

Deep nuclei, from lateral to medial ("Don't Eat Greasy Food"): Dentate (largest; planning and coordination of voluntary movement), Emboliform and Globose (together the interposed nuclei; limb movement), Fastigial (most medial; balance and posture through vestibular connections). They receive Purkinje cell input and send the cerebellum's output through the peduncles.

Afferent fibres:

  • Mossy fibres: from the spinal cord, vestibular nuclei and pontine nuclei; end on granule cells in glomeruli; each excites many granule cells, which reach Purkinje cells through parallel fibres. Carry a wide range of sensory and motor signals.
  • Climbing fibres: only from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus; each wraps one Purkinje cell with hundreds of excitatory synapses; signal movement errors for motor learning.

Three paired arteries:

  • Superior cerebellar artery (SCA): from the basilar artery.
  • Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA): from the basilar artery.
  • Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA): from the vertebral artery.

Veins: superior and inferior cerebellar veins, draining into the superior petrosal, transverse and straight sinuses.

DivisionAnatomyInputOutputRole
Vestibulocerebellum (archicerebellum)Flocculonodular lobeVestibular apparatus and nucleiVestibular nucleiEquilibrium, balance, eye movements (vestibulo-ocular reflex)
Spinocerebellum (paleocerebellum)Vermis and intermediate zonesSpinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts)Fastigial and interposed nucleiMuscle tone, posture, coordination of trunk and limb movements
Cerebrocerebellum (neocerebellum)Lateral hemispheres; the largest divisionCerebral cortex via pontine nucleiDentate nucleus → thalamus → motor cortexPlanning, initiation and timing of skilled voluntary movements; cognitive functions

• Each hemisphere controls the same side of the body: signs are ipsilateral. A right hemisphere lesion gives right-sided limb dysmetria.
  • Flocculonodular (vestibulocerebellum) damage: loss of equilibrium and an unsteady gait.
  • Lateral zone damage: errors in skilled, planned voluntary movements.
  • Midline (vermis) damage: disturbed whole-body movements, trunk and gait.
  • Upper part damage: gait problems and leg incoordination (ataxia).
  • Tonsillar herniation: raised pressure pushes the tonsils into the foramen magnum, compressing the medulla and threatening breathing and circulation. It is life-threatening.

The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and the highest level of control. Hold three layers in mind: the cortex on the surface (grey matter), the white matter under it, and the basal ganglia buried deep inside.

Two sulci map the surface: the central sulcus separates frontal from parietal, and the lateral sulcus puts the temporal lobe below.

The deepest grooves, sulci, delimit the lobes; shallower ones delimit the gyri.

Lateral face: the central sulcus of Rolando (frontal from parietal); the lateral sulcus of Sylvius (frontal and parietal from temporal), with the insula folded deep inside; the parieto-occipital sulcus; and the inconstant pre-occipital notch.

Internal face: the calloso-marginal fissure, the internal parieto-occipital sulcus, and the calcarine fissure, running from the occipital pole and separating the fifth from the sixth occipital gyrus.

LobeGyri and features
Frontal40 percent of the hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus; four gyri: precentral, superior, middle, inferior frontal
ParietalBetween the central, lateral and parieto-occipital sulci; three gyri: postcentral, superior and inferior parietal. The inferior parietal gyrus forms Wernicke's area
OccipitalSix gyri; the sixth, on the internal face, is the cuneus
TemporalFive gyri; the fifth, the hippocampal convolution, curves forward into the uncus
InsulaAt the bottom of the Sylvian fissure; anterior lobule with 3 convolutions, posterior with 2

Telencephalic commissures

  • Corpus callosum: about 200 million fibres joining the hemispheres; the genu ending in the rostrum in front, the splenium behind.
  • Fornix: a C-shaped bundle under the corpus callosum, the largest hippocampal pathway; anterior columns to the mammillary bodies, posterior columns to the hippocampus.
  • Anterior commissure in front of the fornix and callosal genu; posterior commissure under the epiphysis in the back wall of the third ventricle. Functions: cognition, memory, emotion.

Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The left hemisphere handles speech, comprehension, arithmetic and writing; the right creativity, spatial, artistic and musical skills. The left is dominant for hand use and language in about 92 percent of people.

LobeFunctions
FrontalPersonality, behaviour, emotion; judgement and planning; speech production (Broca); movement (motor strip); intelligence and self-awareness
ParietalInterpreting language; touch, pain, temperature (sensory strip); integrating vision, hearing, motor and memory signals; spatial perception
OccipitalVision: colour, light, movement
TemporalUnderstanding language (Wernicke); memory; hearing; sequencing
InsulaTaste, visceral sensation, pain; autonomic control; emotion, empathy; speech articulation and swallowing

Pyramidal tract. The corticospinal tract starts mainly in the primary motor cortex, runs through the internal capsule and cerebral peduncles, and most fibres cross in the medulla.

Language. Wernicke's area in the posterior superior temporal lobe is linked to Broca's area by a neural pathway.

Localising signs: aphasia, blindness, hemiplegia, behavioural disorders and epilepsy. Explored with CT, MRI, EEG, functional MRI and tractography; neurosurgery uses landmarks, mapping and awake surgery.

The cerebrum is the cerebral hemispheres (cortex, subcortical structures, lateral ventricles) plus the diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, third ventricle).

It sits in the cerebral lodge bounded by dura: the vault above, the anterior and middle cranial fossae and tentorium below, wrapped in meninges carrying CSF.

Separated fromBy
The other hemisphereThe falx cerebri
The cerebellumThe tentorium cerebelli
The brainstemThe fissure of Bichat

The tentorium divides the cranial cavity into a supratentorial compartment for the cerebrum and an infratentorial one for the cerebellum and brainstem. The foramen of Pacchioni, its small circumference, is where diencephalon meets midbrain.

Dimensions: ovoid, 14 cm wide, 16 cm long, 12 cm high; weight 1200 to 1400 g; greyish white; soft and crumbly. Each hemisphere has three faces: convex external, concave inferior and flat internal.

Grey matter, grey from its neuron bodies, lies in the peripheral cortex and the deep basal ganglia. White matter, myelinated axons, forms the centrum semiovale and the capsules. The lateral ventricles open into the third ventricle through the foramina of Monro.

White matterLocation
Centrum semiovaleAbove the lateral ventricles and corpus callosum, under the cortex
Internal capsuleBetween thalamus and caudate medially and lentiform nucleus laterally
External capsuleBetween lentiform nucleus and claustrum
Extreme capsuleOutside the claustrum

Cerebral cortex: 3 to 4 mm thick, about 10 billion neurons; it interprets sensation, produces thought, controls behaviour and perceives the world.

Basal ganglia

Subcortical nuclei for motor control, plus motor learning, executive function, behaviour and emotion; part of the extrapyramidal system. They need dopamine.

NucleusKey facts
CaudateC-shaped, in front of the thalamus, lateral to the lateral ventricle; head, body and tail. The head forms the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle; the tail the roof of its inferior horn, ending at the amygdala
PutamenThe most lateral on axial section; lateral to globus pallidus, medial to the external capsule; separated from the caudate by the internal capsule
Globus pallidusMedial to the putamen; split into external and internal segments
Subthalamic nucleusLuys' body, at the diencephalon-midbrain junction; a Parkinson's neurostimulation target
Substantia nigraIn the front of the midbrain between peduncle and tegmentum; pars compacta and pars reticulata

Groupings. Dorsal striatum: caudate plus putamen. Ventral striatum: nucleus accumbens and olfactory tubercle. Lentiform nucleus: putamen plus globus pallidus.

Function. They take the movement plan from the cortex, adjust it, and send it via the thalamus back to the cortex, then down the pyramidal tracts. They also help with planning, memory, eye movements, reward and motivation.

Movement is controlled by two systems working together. The pyramidal system is the fast, direct line for voluntary movement: two neurons, cortex to cord. The extrapyramidal system works in the background: tone, balance, posture and the automatic parts of movement.

The one fact to hold onto: the corticospinal tract crosses in the lower medulla, which is why a brain lesion weakens the opposite side of the body.

A network of nuclei and tracts influencing skeletal muscle for involuntary movement, balance, posture and coordination.

ComponentRole
Cerebral cortexNeurons throughout, mostly in the motor area and nearby frontal and parietal gyri, projecting to the basal nuclei and brainstem
Basal gangliaStriatum (caudate, putamen), globus pallidus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus: motor control, coordination, motor learning
DiencephalonThe subthalamus: entopeduncular nucleus, zona incerta, subthalamic nucleus. None project directly to the cord
CerebellumCoordinates voluntary movement, posture, balance and motor learning
Brainstem nucleiReticular formation (tone, posture, reflexes), red nucleus (coordination), vestibular nuclei (balance)

The extrapyramidal tracts are a multisynaptic system controlled by a basal ganglia motor loop.

TractOriginCrosses?Role
Vestibulospinal (medial, lateral)Vestibular nucleiNoBalance and posture via anti-gravity muscles: arm flexors, leg extensors
Reticulospinal, medialPonsNoFacilitates voluntary movement, increases tone
Reticulospinal, lateralMedullaNoInhibits voluntary movement, reduces tone
OlivospinalInferior oliveNoSynergistic upper limb muscles; cervical enlargement only
RubrospinalRed nucleusYesThought to aid fine hand control
TectospinalSuperior colliculusYesCoordinates head movement with vision; ends at cervical levels

Basal ganglia and cerebellum have rich direct connections both ways, plus a multisynaptic route through the thalamus, and influence dopamine release.

Functional neuroanatomy relates the structure of the nervous system to how it controls sensation, movement and behaviour. It helps interpret neurological symptoms and localise lesions.

The descending tracts carry motor signals from the brain to the lower motor neurons in the cord, controlling voluntary and involuntary movement. They start mainly in the cerebral cortex and brainstem nuclei.

SystemControls
PyramidalVoluntary control of the muscles of body and face
ExtrapyramidalInvoluntary, automatic control of all muscles: tone, balance, posture, locomotion

The two work together to modulate the alpha and gamma motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle.

Alpha and gamma motor neurons sit in the ventral horn. Alpha, the largest in the nervous system, supply skeletal muscle; gamma supply the intrafusal fibres of the muscle spindle. They are arranged somatotopically: medial neurons for proximal muscles, lateral ones for distal muscles.

The control hierarchy. Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex plan and direct movement; brainstem centres handle basic movement and posture. The basal ganglia gate the initiation of movement; the cerebellum coordinates ongoing movement. All act through local circuits on the lower motor neurons that drive the muscles.

TransmitterSource and roleClinical
DopamineSubstantia nigra pars compacta, acting on the striatum; smooths voluntary movementDeficiency (Parkinson's): rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia. Excess: involuntary movements
AcetylcholineExcitatory, from striatal cholinergic interneurons; balances dopamineRelative excess in Parkinson's gives tremor and rigidity; anticholinergics help
GABAMain inhibitory transmitter; striatum, pallidus, nigra pars reticulataDysfunction: chorea, dystonia
GlutamateMain excitatory transmitter; subthalamic and cortical neuronsOveractivity: excitotoxicity
Serotonin, noradrenalineBrainstem modulation of tone, arousal and stabilitySerotonin imbalance adds movement and psychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's

Clinical significance, shown in the lecture: hemiplegia, the parkinsonian gait and the cerebellar gait.

A fast pathway of two neurons: N1, the upper motor neuron (pyramidal cells), and N2, the lower motor neuron (the radicular cells of the ventral horn, or the cells of the brainstem motor nuclei). Named after the medullary pyramids. Two subdivisions: corticospinal tracts for the body and corticobulbar tracts for head and neck.

Corticospinal tracts

Origin. Mainly the primary motor cortex, plus the premotor cortex and supplementary motor area. The voluntary motor cortex is the precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4. The size of each area follows the precision of movement, not muscle size, so hand and tongue areas are largest.

Architecture. Six layers, I to VI. Layer IV is almost absent in the motor cortex. Layer V holds the Betz cells, the origin of the tract.

Course. From the upper two thirds of the precentral gyrus, the fibres descend through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, behind the geniculate tract, then the middle of the cerebral peduncle. They split into fascicles in the pons and reconverge as the pyramid in the medulla. Decussation occurs at the bulbospinal junction.

TractCrossingEndsSupplies
Lateral corticospinalAbout 90 percent cross in the lower medullaVentral horn at all levelsLimb muscles
Anterior corticospinalIpsilateral, then crosses at the segmentVentral horn, cervical and upper thoracicAxial trunk muscles

Corticobulbar tracts

The corticonuclear or geniculate pathway links the motor cortex to the cranial nerve nuclei. It passes through the genu of the internal capsule, hence its name, then the middle of the cerebral peduncle between the substantia nigra and the interpeduncular space. It supplies the striated muscles of head and neck. Its fibres cross gradually as they descend: some to the nuclei of III, IV and VI, others to the motor nuclei of V, VII, IX, X and XI.

The diencephalon sits at the centre of the brain, wrapped around the third ventricle. It has four parts, and each has one job worth remembering:

PartKey job
ThalamusRelays nearly every sensation to the cortex: the gateway to the cortex
HypothalamusHomeostasis and control of the pituitary
EpithalamusThe pineal gland and melatonin
SubthalamusMotor control with the basal ganglia

The posterior segment of the diencephalon, at the back of the roof of the third ventricle. It consists of the stria medullaris, the posterior commissure, the habenular nuclei, the pineal body and the paraventricular nuclei. It links the limbic system to the rest of the brain.

  • Stria medullaris thalami: fibres from near the anterior pole of the thalamus back to the habenular trigone. The habenular commissure links the amygdaloid and hippocampal complexes of both sides.
  • Habenula: a pair of small nuclei above the back of the thalamus, near the midline.
  • Pineal gland: a small piriform outgrowth of the back wall of the third ventricle, below the splenium, between the two superior colliculi. Its pinealocytes secrete melatonin in response to darkness, driving circadian rhythms.

Clinical: epithalamic dysfunction is linked to major depression, schizophrenia and sleep disorders; low melatonin tends to cause mood disorders. Pineal tumours also occur here.

Below the thalamus, forming the floor of the third ventricle: a small cone projecting down into the infundibulum, which joins the pituitary gland. Three regions: supraoptic, tuberal and mammillary.

Functions. Homeostasis: hunger, thirst, body temperature, blood pressure and heart rate. It is the interface between the nervous and endocrine systems, regulates sexual activity and controls the stress response.

Damage can cause aggression, acute stress, hypothermia or hyperthermia, fatigue, weight change and altered sex drive.

A small region between thalamus and midbrain, important for motor control through its links with the basal ganglia.

BoundaryStructure
AboveThalamus
BelowMidbrain
MedialHypothalamus
LateralInternal capsule
PosteriorRed nucleus and substantia nigra
StructureRole
Subthalamic nucleusLens-shaped, medial to the internal capsule; part of the basal ganglia circuit; modulates the globus pallidus and substantia nigra
Zona incertaPoorly defined area above the nucleus; sensorimotor integration
Fields of ForelFibre bundles linking globus pallidus, thalamus and subthalamic nucleus
Subthalamic fasciculusLinks the nucleus to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra

How it controls movement. Its glutamatergic neurons excite the internal globus pallidus, whose GABAergic neurons inhibit the thalamus and so inhibit movement. A lesion removes that brake, causing hemiballismus. It is a target of deep brain stimulation.

Your professor's review questions: the pons is not part of the diencephalon; the pineal gland belongs to the epithalamus; the thalamus is the main sensory relay except for smell; the hypothalamus controls autonomic and endocrine activity; the subthalamic nucleus is for motor control.

A paired grey matter structure between cortex and midbrain, made of nuclei separated by white matter laminae, connecting to the cortex in all directions. The two thalami are joined by the interthalamic adhesion. It is ovoid and narrowest in front.

A Y-shaped internal medullary lamina divides it into anterior, medial and lateral parts. The pulvinar is the posterior nuclear group.

Geniculate bodyRelaysRoute
Lateral (LGB)VisionRetina via the optic tract, to the occipital cortex via the optic radiations
Medial (MGB)HearingInferior colliculus, to the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe
RelationStructures
AnteriorIts pole forms the back wall of the foramen of Monro; five veins join there as the internal cerebral vein
MedialForms the lateral wall of the third ventricle
SuperiorChoroid plexus of the third ventricle, body of the fornix, internal cerebral vein, caudate nucleus, posterior limb of the internal capsule
PosteriorThe pulvinar, lateral to the pineal gland, habenula, posterior commissure, corpora quadrigemina and splenium
InferiorHypothalamus, cerebral aqueduct, midbrain tegmentum

Functions: consciousness and sleep; filtering all sensation except smell before it reaches the cortex; and modulating motor responses via the basal ganglia.

Blood supply: the posterior cerebral artery, in four territories: anterior, inferolateral, paramedian and posterior.

The ear turns vibrating air into vibrating fluid. The external ear collects sound, the middle ear amplifies it across the air-to-fluid gap, and the inner ear, covered in Part 2, transduces it into nerve signals.

The middle ear is where most exam questions live: its six walls, each with a dangerous neighbour, and its three ossicles.

The pinna (auricle) and the external auditory canal. It localises sound, contributes to amplification and protects the deeper ear; it also matters aesthetically.

Situation. Behind the temporomandibular joint and the parotid region, in front of the mastoid, below the temporal region. The pinna is fixed to the skull by its anterior third; its posterior two thirds are mobile.

Lateral surface. Four constant projections: the helix around the upper two thirds; the anthelix, bifid and concentric to it, separated by the scapha; the tragus; and the antitragus. The concha is a depression bounded by the anthelix behind and above, the root of the helix and the tragus in front and the antitragus below: its upper posterior part is the cymba conchae, its lower anterior part the cavum conchae. The lobe is a skin fold with no cartilage.

Muscles, rudimentary in humans. Extrinsic: auricularis anterior and superior from the epicranial aponeurosis, auricularis posterior from the mastoid process to the eminentia conchae. Intrinsic: small muscles between the cartilages.

Cartilaginous partBony part
ShareOuter third, 8 mmInner two thirds, 16 mm
SkinThick, with hair and ceruminous glandsThin, continuous with the drum, no hair or glands
NoteContinuous with the auricular cartilageContains the isthmus

The canal is 25 mm long, 8 mm wide and S-shaped. To examine it and the drum, pull the pinna upwards, backwards and laterally. Arteries: superficial temporal and posterior auricular. Nerves: superficial cervical plexus, VII bis and the trigeminal nerve.

title: The middle ear and tympanic cavity
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
An air cavity in the temporal bone with three parts: the Eustachian tube in front, the tympanic cavity in the centre and the mastoid cells behind.

The tympanic cavity is a six-sided box, five bony walls plus the membranous lateral wall. Length 15 mm, height 15 to 7 mm, width 3 to 6 mm; a biconcave disc in coronal section.

WallFeatures and relations
LateralFour fifths tympanic membrane; separates the cavity from the external canal
Medial (labyrinthine)Divided by the facial canal prominence. Above: the lateral semicircular canal prominence. Below: the promontory, oval window and round window
Roof (tegmen tympani)Thin bone separating the cavity from the middle cranial fossa
FloorThin bone over the jugular bulb; sometimes deficient, leaving the bulb covered only by mucosa
AnteriorThin bone over the internal carotid artery below; above, the canals for tensor tympani and the auditory tube
PosteriorSeparates the cavity from the mastoid antrum and cells; the aditus ad antrum; the vertical facial canal behind the pyramid down to the stylomastoid foramen; the retrotympanum below

The tympanic membrane. Thin, semi-transparent, pearly white or slightly pink: height 10 mm, width 9 mm, thickness 0.05 to 0.09 mm. Surface features: the malleus, its lateral process, the cone of light and the sulcus tympanicus. Three layers: outer stratified squamous, middle fibrous (enclosing the malleus handle, with radiating and circular fibres), inner low columnar mucosa. The pars tensa forms most of it, rimmed by the annulus tympanicus; the pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) is a small lax triangle above the lateral process of the malleus, where loose areolar tissue replaces the fibrous layer.

title: Ossicles, mastoid, Eustachian tube and nerves
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
OssicleParts
MalleusHead, neck, manubrium, lateral process, anterior process
IncusBody, short process, long process, lenticular process
StapesThe smallest and lightest, about 2 mg: head, anterior crus, posterior crus, footplate

Mastoid cells. Air cells in the mastoid bone; the antrum is the largest; all communicate with each other and with the tympanic cavity.

Eustachian tube. Osseocartilaginous, from the tympanic cavity downwards, forwards and medially to the nasopharynx: a superior posterior bony part and an anterior cartilaginous part. Length 31 to 38 mm, diameter 2 mm. Functions: pressure equalisation, protection and drainage.

Tympanic plexus, on the promontory: the tympanic branch of CN IX (Jacobson's nerve), sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus, and a branch from the geniculate ganglion.

title: Physiology of the external and middle ear
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
External ear. The pinna captures sound and helps localise its source. The canal is a resonator amplifying speech frequencies around 2000 to 5000 Hz, and its cerumen traps dust and debris.

Middle ear. The ossicles form a lever system amplifying the drum's vibrations and passing them to the oval window. This overcomes the impedance mismatch between air and cochlear fluid. The mechanical advantage depends on the relative lengths of malleus and incus. Together with the hydraulic pressure ratio, this is the transformer function of the middle ear, which reconstructive surgery must preserve.

Pressure. The Eustachian tube opens on swallowing or yawning to equalise pressure across the drum, preventing barotrauma.

Protection. The acoustic (stapes) reflex contracts the ossicular muscles in response to loud sounds, reducing energy reaching the inner ear.

The inner ear is a set of tubes inside tubes. The outer bony labyrinth holds perilymph; the inner membranous labyrinth holds endolymph and carries the sensors.

Front for hearing, back for balance: the cochlea hears, while the vestibule and semicircular canals sense position and movement.

• Just in front of the vestibule, shaped like a snail shell.
  • A bony tube 30 mm long, 1 to 2 mm in diameter.
  • A central pillar, the modiolus, and a bony cochlear canal.

Modiolus. The axial bony stem around which the canal spirals, like an elongated cone. Its base lies at the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus and is perforated by the cochlear nerve; its apex points toward the middle ear under the apical turn.

Cochlear canal. Spirals around the modiolus in two and three quarter turns; its basal turn bulges into the tympanic cavity as the promontory. The bony spiral lamina projects from the modiolus like a screw thread, partly dividing the canal into scala vestibuli above and scala tympani below, which meet at the apex through the helicotrema.

At the basal turn, the scala vestibuli communicates with the vestibule. The scala tympani presents the round window, below and behind the promontory, closed by the secondary tympanic membrane, and the start of the aqueduct of the cochlea, joining cochlear perilymph to the CSF.

The cochlear duct lies in the bony cochlea, the saccule and utricle in the vestibule, and the three semicircular ducts in the canals. Connections:

  • The cochlear duct (basal turn) joins the saccule by the ductus reuniens.
  • The saccule and utricle are joined by the Y-shaped utriculo-saccular duct, which expands into the endolymphatic duct and sac.
  • The utricle connects to the three semicircular ducts by five openings.
ReceptorLocationFunctionNerve
Spiral organ of CortiCochlear ductHearingCochlear nerve
MaculaeSaccule and utricleStatic balanceVestibular nerve
Cristae ampullarisSemicircular ductsKinetic balanceVestibular nerve

The cochlear duct is the spiral anterior part, two and three quarter turns, 30 mm long, between scala vestibuli and scala tympani. It contains the organ of Corti.

Organ of Corti, on the basilar membrane. Hair cells carry stereocilia overlaid by the tectorial membrane. Inner hair cells are richly supplied by cochlear nerve fibres and transmit auditory impulses. Outer hair cells take efferent fibres and modulate the inner hair cells. Supporting cells and the tectorial membrane complete it.

The travelling wave. Sound starts at the oval window and travels up the scala vestibuli toward the apex; its amplitude peaks at frequency-specific sites, where the organ of Corti is stimulated.

Saccule and utricle. The saccule is a small globular sac; the utricle an oblong sac, larger than the saccule.

Highly differentiated organs for hearing and balance, inside the massive petrous bone. Two main parts:

Bony labyrinthMembranous labyrinth
PartsVestibule, semicircular canals, cochleaSemicircular ducts, cochlear duct, utricle, saccule
FluidPerilymph, between the two labyrinthsEndolymph, inside
NatureBony cavities lined by periosteum, from the otic capsuleA closed system of epithelial sacs and ducts

The anterior labyrinth, for hearing, is the cochlear duct. The posterior labyrinth, for balance, is the utricle, saccule, semicircular ducts and endolymphatic system.

title: Central pathways, nerves and blood supply
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
Auditory pathway. Cochlea, cochlear nuclei, olivary nuclei, lateral lemniscus nuclei, inferior colliculi, medial geniculate, acoustic radiation, auditory cortex in the transverse temporal gyrus. The main pathway is contralateral, with a minor ipsilateral one.

Vestibular connections. To the cerebellum; to the oculomotor and abducens nuclei via the medial longitudinal fasciculus for the eye-movement reflex; and to the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal tract for posture.

CN VIII divides in the internal auditory canal into an anterior cochlear nerve and a posterior vestibular nerve.

Cochlear nerve. Voluminous, through the IAC into the cochlear fossa, ending at the spiral ganglion of Corti along the turns of the spiral canal. Inner hair cells connect to about 45,000 afferent fibres, 90 to 95 percent of the nerve. Outer hair cells are contractile rather than true receptors, increasing frequency selectivity.

Vestibular branchSupplies
Superior vestibular nerveUtricular nerve to the utricular macula; superior ampullary nerve to the superior canal crest; lateral ampullary nerve to the lateral canal crest
Inferior vestibular nerveSaccular nerve to the saccular macula
Posterior ampullary nerveThe crest of the posterior canal

Blood supply. The labyrinthine artery, from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery or directly from the basilar trunk.

Clinical applications: hearing and balance disorders, for example deafness.

The vestibule is the central ovoid cavity between the cochlea in front and the semicircular canals behind, medial to the middle ear. Its lateral wall meets the middle ear at the oval window, closed by the stapes footplate and the annular ligament.

The semicircular canals: anterior (superior), posterior and lateral, in three planes at 90 degrees. Each is about two thirds of a circle, dilated at one end into an ampulla.

CanalPlaneOpenings
AnteriorVerticalAmpullated end opens anterolaterally; the other end joins the posterior canal's as the crus commune
PosteriorVerticalLower ampullated end opens into the vestibule; upper end forms the crus commune
LateralHorizontalBoth ends open directly into the vestibule; the ampullated end lies near the anterior canal's

So the three canals open into the vestibule by five openings.

Why it is needed. Nearly parallel rays come from a distant object, but divergent rays come from a close one. From a near object those rays would focus behind the retina if the ciliary muscle stayed relaxed, giving blurred vision. The solution is to increase the curvature and refractive power of the lens.

The lens itself. In a young person the lens has a strong elastic capsule filled with viscous, proteinaceous but transparent fluid. Relaxed, with no tension on its capsule, it takes an almost spherical shape, mainly through the elastic retraction of the capsule.

Near object (accommodation)Near to far
1. Ciliary muscles contract1. Far object focused on the retina
2. The suspensory ligament relaxes2. The dioptric power of the eye decreases
3. The lens becomes more convex3. The lens becomes less convex (flat)
4. The dioptric power of the eye increases4. The suspensory ligament contracts (taut)
5. The near object is focused on the retina

The near response has three linked parts: lens changes (accommodation), changes in the pupil, and convergence of the eyes. Its goal is clear vision of a nearby object.

The accommodation reflex. Afferent: retina, optic nerve, optic chiasma, optic tract, lateral geniculate body, visual cortex. Efferent: oculomotor nucleus, parasympathetic fibres, ciliary ganglion, ciliary muscle, circular pupillary muscle.

Cones (photopic)Rods (scotopic)
LightBright light visionNight and dim light vision
AcuityHigh visual acuity: colours and detailsLow visual acuity: no colours or details
SensitivityLow sensitivity to light: needs a high visual threshold to be stimulatedGreat sensitivity to light: low visual threshold

This lecture is about wiring. Which nerves reach the eye, and what circuits they form.

Four reflexes carry most of it: the pupillary light reflex, the accommodation reflex, the corneal reflex and the autonomic control of the lacrimal gland. For each one, ask the same two questions: what is the afferent limb, and what is the efferent limb? Get those and the rest is detail.

GroupNerves
SensoryI, II, VIII (remember 128)
MotorIII, IV, VI, XI, XII (remember 346, 11, 12)
MixedV, VII, IX, X
Carrying parasympathetic fibresIII, VII, IX, X

The optic nerve. Unlike other cranial nerves it is wrapped in the meninges: dura, subdural space, arachnoid, subarachnoid space containing CSF, and pia. It behaves like a tract of the brain.

Orders of neuron in the visual pathway: first order, the cone and rod photoreceptors; second order, the bipolar cells leading to the ganglion cells of the optic nerve; third order, the neuron from the lateral geniculate body to the cerebral cortex.

The chain: cones and rods, bipolar cells, ganglion cells, optic nerve, optic chiasma, optic tract, lateral geniculate body in the thalamus, geniculocalcarine tract, optic radiation, visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) in the occipital cortex.

Touch on the cornea travels in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V) to the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, then to the facial motor nucleus on both sides. The temporal branch of the facial nerve (VII) makes the orbicularis oculi contract, so both eyes blink.

The orbicularis oculi is supplied by the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve.

title: Autonomic control of the lacrimal gland
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
LimbPathwayEffect
ParasympatheticFacial nerve, greater superficial petrosal nerve, pterygoid canal, pterygopalatine ganglion, then the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves to the glandStimulates secretion
SympatheticInternal carotid plexus, deep petrosal nerve, joining the same route through the pterygoid canalInhibits secretion
SensoryLacrimal nerve, a branch of V1, through the trigeminal ganglionSensation

The ciliary ganglion carries three kinds of fibre: parasympathetic (which synapse there, arriving by the motor root from the inferior division of CN III), sympathetic (from the carotid plexus) and sensory (from the nasociliary nerve). The sympathetic and sensory fibres pass straight through. Its branches are the short ciliary nerves.

Afferent pathway

  • Light enters the pupil and stimulates the retina.
  • Retinal ganglion cells transmit the light signal to the optic nerve.
  • The optic nerve enters the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibres cross to the contralateral optic tract, while the temporal retinal fibres stay in the ipsilateral optic tract.
  • Fibres from the optic tracts project to and synapse in the pretectal nuclei in the dorsal midbrain, in the collicular region.
  • The pretectal nuclei project to the ipsilateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus and also to the contralateral one via the posterior commissure.

Efferent pathway

  • The Edinger-Westphal nucleus projects preganglionic parasympathetic fibres, which exit the midbrain and travel along the oculomotor nerve (CN III), then synapse on postganglionic fibres in the ciliary ganglion.
  • Those postganglionic fibres, the short ciliary nerves, innervate the sphincter muscle of the pupil, producing pupillary constriction.

The result. Light shone in one eye constricts the pupil of that eye (direct reflex) and of the other eye (consensual reflex). In darkness the reflex becomes inhibited, giving dilation of the pupil in both eyes.

The seven steps: I. projection of light. II. optic nerve. III. pretectal nucleus. IV. Edinger-Westphal nucleus. V. oculomotor nerve. VI. ciliary ganglion. VII. short ciliary nerve.

The lecture lists what has to be covered: motor supply CN III, parasympathetic supply CN III, motor supply CN IV, motor supply CN VI, the pupillary light reflex, the accommodation reflex, the corneal reflex, and autonomic control of the lacrimal gland.

Trochlear nerve palsy. The trochlear nucleus sits in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. An infarct in the left midbrain produces a left CN IV palsy.

Abducens nerve palsy. The abducens nucleus contains two types of cell: motor neurons that control the lateral rectus muscle on the same side, and interneurons that cross the midline and connect to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus, which controls the medial rectus of the opposite eye.

Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). It links CN III, CN IV, CN VI and CN VIII with the cerebellum, producing conjugate movement of the eyes and coordinating them with head movement.

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
• Discuss the cranial nerves associated with the eye.
  • Relate the visual pathway to image formation.
  • Discuss the pathways of the accommodation reflex, pupillary light reflex and corneal reflex and relate them to their functions.
  • Discuss the effects of infarcts on the central nervous system.

A clear plasma-derived ultrafiltrate, normally devoid of proteins, cells or other macromolecules.

Functions

  • Delivery of oxygen and nutrients, and removal of waste products, inflammatory products and other cellular debris from the posterior cornea and crystalline lens.
  • Provision of a low refractive index transparent medium between the lens and cornea.
  • Maintenance of intraocular pressure for the optimal shape and alignment of ocular structures.

Formation

By diffusion, ultrafiltration and active secretion. Diffusion and ultrafiltration form a reservoir of plasma in the ciliary stroma. Active secretion of aqueous from that ultrafiltrate occurs across the ciliary epithelium and is relatively pressure independent. Ascorbic acid, amino acids and glucose are transported into the aqueous to supply the cornea and lens.

Passage and drainage

Aqueous is formed by the ciliary body and secreted into the posterior chamber. It traverses the pupil to enter the anterior chamber and exits by one of two drainage pathways.

RouteHow it worksPressure
Trabecular meshworkAqueous traverses the meshwork, crosses the inner wall of Schlemm's canal, then passes into collector channels, aqueous veins and episcleral veins. Accounts for 50 to 75 percent of drainage.Pressure sensitive: outflow increases with greater intraocular pressure
UveoscleralAqueous passes freely from the anterior chamber angle into the connective tissue spaces within the ciliary muscle, via the iris root and anterior face of the ciliary body. This pathway may increase with age.Pressure independent: consistently less than intraocular pressure and constant, so it keeps draining despite fluctuations

Inflammation causes the trabecular meshwork to become clogged with inflammatory cells and debris, reducing trabecular outflow. Locally produced prostaglandins enhance uveoscleral drainage, preventing dangerously high intraocular pressure.

Intraocular pressure

The medical term for fluid pressure inside the eyes, and an important part of vision and eye health. The chamber behind the eye is filled with vitreous humour, a thick gel-like material. Aqueous humour fills the space at the front, between the cornea and the iris, and is thinner and more watery. The body constantly makes and drains aqueous, and pressure reflects that balance. It is measured with a tonometer.

The eyeball is three coats wrapped around a fluid-filled ball: a tough fibrous outer layer (sclera and cornea), a vascular middle layer (the uvea: iris, ciliary body, choroid) and a neural inner layer (the retina).

Two currents run through it. Light passes through the four refractive media on its way to the retina. Aqueous fluid is made by the ciliary body, flows through the pupil, and drains away again. When that drainage fails, pressure rises: glaucoma.

The cornea forms one sixth of the outer coat; the sclera forms five sixths. The episclera is the outermost layer of the sclera, of loose fibrous elastic tissue, attaching to Tenon's capsule. Between the bulbar conjunctiva and the sclera lies a vascular plexus with superficial and deep episcleral vessels.

CorneaSclera
Higher convexityRelatively avascular
Completely avascularProvides insertion for the muscles
Nourished by the lacrimal gland outside and aqueous humour insideLess sensitive
Highly sensitive (CN V1)Arrangement of collagens allows for less hydration

Clinical correlates

Scleral icterus (yellow eyes), also called icteric sclera, is a yellowing of the white of the eye, associated with hepatitis and other liver diseases.

Scleritis is inflammation of both the episclera and the underlying sclera. Up to 50 percent of cases involve an underlying systemic disease such as rheumatoid arthritis. Onset is gradual, with severe piercing eye pain developing over several days that tends to worsen with eye movement. It usually begins in one area and spreads until the entire sclera is involved.

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
• Discuss the layers of the eyeball and their functions.
  • Relate the formation of aqueous humour to its drainage and the maintenance of intraocular pressure.
  • Discuss the structures that act as refractive media of the eye.
  • Briefly discuss the clinical correlates of all these structures.

Tenon's capsule, the fascial sheath of the eyeball, is a thin membrane enveloping the eye from the optic nerve to the corneal limbus. It separates the eye from the orbital fat and forms a socket in which it moves.

title: Refractive media: cornea, aqueous, lens, vitreous
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
The four refractive media in order: I. the cornea, II. the aqueous humour, III. the lens, IV. the vitreous humour.

The lens

Transparent, biconvex and enclosed in a capsule, which is suspended by zonular fibres, the suspensory ligament of the lens. Maximum refraction occurs through the cornea, not the lens. In the absence of nerve stimulation, more distant objects come into focus.

In the presence of nerve stimulation (CN III, parasympathetic): sphincter-like contraction of the ciliary muscles, the ring becomes smaller, the zonules relax, the lens relaxes and thickens, giving accommodation for near vision. Lens thickness increases with age, leading to less ability to accommodate.

Histology. A biconvex structure of great elasticity, a feature lost with age as the lens hardens. Three principal components:

  1. Lens capsule: a thick, homogeneous, refractile, carbohydrate-rich coating on the outer surface of the epithelial cells. A very thick basement membrane of type IV collagen and glycoprotein.
  2. Subcapsular epithelium: a single layer of cuboidal cells, present only on the anterior surface of the lens.
  3. Lens fibres: highly differentiated cells filled with crystallins. They permit focusing on near and far objects by changing the curvature of the lens. At rest or far gaze the lens is stretched or flat; to focus near, the lens thickens.

Cataract. The eye's natural lens becomes cloudy as proteins in the lens break down, making things look blurry, hazy or less colourful. Symptoms: cloudy, blurry, foggy or filmy vision; changes in colour perception; sensitivity to bright sunlight, headlights or lamps; glare, including halos or streaks around lights; and difficulty seeing at night. Surgery: an incision is made, emulsification breaks up the cloudy lens, an intraocular lens is implanted, and the incision heals on its own.

Vitreous humour

A watery fluid enclosed in the meshes of the vitreous body, a jelly-like substance filling up 80 percent of the posterior segment of the eyeball, also called the postremal or vitreous chamber. Functions: transmitting light, and holding the retina and lens in their respective places.

The retina is the inner layer and consists of two portions: a posterior, photosensitive portion and an anterior, non-photosensitive portion, the inner lining of the ciliary body and posterior part of the iris.

PartNote
Neural layerLight-receptive; ends anteriorly along the ora serrata
Pigmented cell layerA single layer of cells that absorbs light to reduce scattering within the eye
Optic disc (papilla)Known as the blind spot: no photoreceptors. Located in the fundus of the retina, where the sensory fibres of the optic nerve enter the eyeball
MaculaContains special photoreceptor cones for visual acuity; lacks blood vessels
FoveaAt the centre of the macula; responsible for high-acuity vision; densely saturated with cone photoreceptors

Signalling. Photoreceptors and bipolar cells produce graded potentials rather than action potentials. Ganglion cells generate action potentials, and their axons join together to form the optic nerve, which exits through the back of the eye at the optic disc.

RodsCones
Light levelLow light: scotopic visionHigher light: photopic vision
ColourNo colour visionColour vision
AcuityLow spatial acuityHigh spatial acuity; the central fovea is exclusively cones
NumberAbout 120 million per retinaAbout 6 million per retina
PigmentRhodopsin (visual purple), bleached by light to initiate the visual stimulusIodopsin, in three types with maximum sensitivity in the red, green or blue region
StructureThin, elongated, two portions. External part: numerous flattened membrane disks stacked like coins. Inner segment: rich in glycogen and mitochondria, near a constriction. The outer segment is the site of photosensitivity; the inner segment holds the metabolic machinerySimilar to rods, with outer and inner segments, a basal body with a cilium, and an accumulation of mitochondria and ribosomes. The three functional types cannot be distinguished morphologically

The uvea, or uveal tract, lies between the sclera and the retina. Anterior portion: the iris and ciliary body. Posterior portion: the choroid.

PartWhat it does
IrisA pigmented diaphragm with a central aperture, the pupil, on the anterior surface of the lens. Sphincter muscles within it adjust pupil size in response to light and the autonomic nervous system.
Ciliary bodyA muscular structure connecting the choroid with the circumference of the iris. It alters the shape and thickness of the lens (accommodation), and its ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour.
ChoroidThe posterior portion of the uvea, between sclera and retina.

The hard palate is made by the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind.

The skull has 22 bones. Eight of them wrap the brain (the neurocranium) and fourteen shape the face, jaws, nose and eye sockets (the viscerocranium). This lecture walks through them one by one, then looks at the underside of the skull and the air-filled sinuses.

The facial bones support the muscles of the face, hold the teeth and surround the orbits, the nasal cavity and the mouth. The mandible is the only bone of the skull that moves (at the temporomandibular joint).

  • The atlas turns on the axis (C2). The atlanto-axial joint allows rotation, the "no" movement.

SinusWhereDrains into
FrontalFrontal bone, behind the eyebrowsMiddle meatus, through the frontonasal duct and infundibulum

Functions (some are debated): lightening the skull, humidifying and warming inhaled air, supporting the immune defence of the nose, and giving resonance to the voice. Three sinuses lie in neurocranial bones (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid). The maxilla is the only facial bone that contains a sinus.

body.html:

Vomer (1)Plough-shaped. Forms the lower and posterior part of the bony nasal septum; meets the palatine, maxilla and ethmoid.
Palatine (2)L-shaped: horizontal plate (posterior hard palate and nasal floor) and perpendicular plate (lateral nasal wall). Adds a small part of the orbital floor. Greater and lesser palatine foramina carry palatine branches of V2.

Lacrimal (2)Small bone on the medial wall of the orbit; helps form the lacrimal fossa and the nasolacrimal groove.

PartWhat to know
BodyCentral, cube-like. Contains the sphenoid sinuses. Its upper surface is the sella turcica (hypophysial fossa for the pituitary, tuberculum sellae in front, dorsum sellae behind).
Greater wingsForm the floor of the middle cranial fossa, part of the lateral skull wall and the back of the lateral orbital wall. Openings: foramen rotundum (V2), foramen ovale (V3), foramen spinosum (middle meningeal vessels).
Lesser wingsSeparate the anterior and middle cranial fossae. Form the lateral border of the optic canal (the body forms the medial border). Carry the anterior clinoid processes. The superior orbital fissure lies between the lesser and greater wings.
Pterygoid processesHang down from where the body meets the greater wing. Each has a medial and a lateral plate, for muscle attachment.

PartWhat to know
Squamous partLarge flat plate on the side of the skull. Origin of temporalis. Its zygomatic process meets the zygomatic bone to form the zygomatic arch. The mandibular fossa below it receives the head of the mandible.
Petrous partDense, pyramid-shaped part that separates the middle and posterior cranial fossae and protects the inner ear. Has the internal acoustic meatus, carotid canal and jugular foramen.
Tympanic partCurved plate that forms much of the external acoustic meatus.
Mastoid partContains the mastoid air cells. The mastoid process is an attachment for sternocleidomastoid.
Mandibular (glenoid) fossaHollow on the underside of the squamous part, behind the articular eminence. It receives the head (condyle) of the mandible at the temporomandibular joint.
Styloid processThin spike pointing down and forward. The stylomastoid foramen just behind it carries the facial nerve. Attachment for stylopharyngeus, styloglossus and stylohyoid.

The pterion is the H-shaped meeting point on the side of the skull of four bones: frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid. It is the thinnest part of the skull wall and lies over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, so a blow there can tear the artery.

The cheekbone. Diamond-shaped, it forms the prominence of the cheek, part of the lateral wall and floor of the orbit, and part of the zygomatic arch.

ProcessRole
FrontalMeets the frontal bone at the frontozygomatic suture; forms the front of the lateral orbital wall
TemporalRuns back to meet the temporal bone and form the zygomatic arch
MaxillaryMeets the maxilla; forms part of the infraorbital rim and orbital floor

It articulates with four bones: frontal, sphenoid (greater wing), temporal and maxilla. Three small foramina (zygomatico-orbital, zygomaticofacial, zygomaticotemporal) are linked by a canal that carries the zygomatic nerve. Zygomaticus major and minor and masseter attach to it.

Two different muscle groups live in this region and it is worth keeping them apart from the first minute.

  • Muscles of facial expression: thin, subcutaneous, inserting into skin, supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). They move the face and guard the openings of the face.
  • Muscles of mastication: thick, attached to bone, supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3). They move the mandible at the temporomandibular joint.

Get the two nerves right and half the lecture falls into place.

Ear: anterior, superior and posterior auricular muscles.

Platysma: origin the upper part of the pectoral and deltoid fascia; its fibres run upward over the clavicle to insert into the base of the mandible and the skin of the lower face and lip. It releases the pressure of the skin on the veins underneath, depresses the mandible and pulls the angle of the mouth downward.

• They control the expressions of the face, which is why they are also called the muscles of facial expression or mimetic muscles.
  • They act as sphincters and dilators of the openings of the face: the eyes, nose and mouth.
  • They are subcutaneous, lying in the superficial fascia, with origins from bone or fascia and insertions into the skin.
  • All of them are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

Orbicularis oris encircles the mouth. It forms an ellipse around the mouth and inserts into the skin and mucous membrane of the lips. Contraction narrows and closes the mouth, as in whistling.

Origin: the posterior parts of the maxilla and mandible and the pterygomandibular raphe, which separates it from the superior constrictor of the pharynx. Insertion: it blends with orbicularis oris and into the lips. It compresses the cheeks so that food is kept under the teeth during chewing, expels air from the distended cheeks as in blowing a trumpet, helps in whistling and smiling, and in newborns is used to suckle.
