• Discuss the muscles of facial expression and their innervation.
  • Relate the muscles of mastication to the actions at the temporomandibular joint.
  • Briefly review the blood supply of the faciomaxillary region.

Epicranius (occipitofrontalis) is a broad musculofibrous sheet covering the vertex from the occipital bone to the eyebrows. Its two bellies are joined by the galea aponeurotica.

MuscleOriginInsertionAction
Occipital bellyTendinous fibres from the lateral two-thirds of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the mastoid part of the temporal boneGalea aponeuroticaDraws the scalp backward
Frontal bellyGalea aponeurotica (no bony attachment)Skin of the eyebrows; medial fibres blend with procerus, lateral fibres with corrugator and orbicularis oculiWrinkles the forehead, raises the eyebrows
Orbicularis oculi, orbital partNasal part of the frontal bone, frontal process of the maxilla, medial palpebral ligamentAn uninterrupted ellipse around the orbitCloses the eye forcefully, wrinkling the forehead; under conscious control
Orbicularis oculi, palpebral partMedial palpebral ligamentLateral palpebral rapheCloses the lids gently, as in blinking or sleep; involuntary
Corrugator superciliiMedial end of the superciliary archSkin of the medial half of the eyebrowDraws the eyebrows medially and downward: the frowning muscle
Levator palpebrae superiorisLesser wing of the sphenoid, above and anterior to the optic canalAnterior surface of the tarsal plate, with fibres to the skin and superior conjunctival fornixRaises the upper eyelid. Nerve: oculomotor (CN III), not CN VII

Articular components: the mandibular fossa and the articular tubercle of the temporal bone, and the condyle (head) of the mandible.

The joint has a unique mechanism: the articular surfaces never touch, because an articular disc splits the joint into two synovial cavities, each lined by its own synovial membrane. The articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.

Ligaments (three extracapsular, all stabilising the joint):

  • Lateral ligament: runs from the articular tubercle to the neck of the mandible. A thickening of the capsule that prevents posterior dislocation.
  • Sphenomandibular ligament: from the spine of the sphenoid to the mandible.
  • Stylomandibular ligament: a thickening of the fascia of the parotid gland.

Movements, split between the two parts of the joint:

  • Upper part: protrusion and retraction, the forward and backward movements of the jaw.
  • Lower part: elevation and depression, closing and opening the mouth. Depression is mostly caused by gravity; the digastric, geniohyoid and mylohyoid assist if there is resistance. Elevation is a strong movement produced by the muscles of mastication.

Dislocation: a blow to the side of the face, yawning or taking a large bite can make the head of the mandible slip out of the mandibular fossa and be pulled anteriorly, so the patient cannot close the mouth. The facial and auriculotemporal nerves run close to the joint and can be damaged if the injury is high energy.

Relations: anteriorly the mandibular notch with the masseteric nerve and artery; posteriorly the tympanic plate of the external acoustic meatus; laterally the parotid gland, fascia and skin; medially the maxillary artery and vein and the auriculotemporal nerve; superiorly the middle cranial fossa with the temporal lobe.

The larynx is a box of nine cartilages held together by joints and ligaments, with muscles that swing the arytenoids to open and close the vocal cords. Everything in this lecture hangs on two questions: which muscle moves the cords which way, and which nerve supplies it.

The two rules that carry most of the exam: the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor, and the cricothyroid is the only muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Nine cartilages. Three unpaired and large: thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis. Three paired and small: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform. The principal ones are the cricoid, the thyroid and the two arytenoids.

CartilageDescription
ThyroidShaped like an open book, open backwards, with two vertical quadrilateral laminae. Each has an anterolateral side, a posteromedial side (smooth, related to the piriform sinus), a superior border with the superior thyroid incisure, an inferior border with the inferior thyroid incisure, and a thick vertical posterior margin extended by the superior and inferior cornua, the inferior carrying a cricoid articular surface
EpiglottisShaped like a tennis racket with a curved lower handle forming its foot. Laryngeal (posterior) side: respiratory mucosa with cribriform depressions, facing the vestibule. Lingual (anterior) side: concave, facing the base of the tongue and hyoid. Base superior and free; vertex or foot inferior, inserting into the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage through the thyroepiglottic ligament
CricoidA signet-shaped ring with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina, at C6. The only cartilage that completely encircles the lumen of the larynx, and the foundation stone of the larynx. The posterior lamina has a median ridge with a depressed area on each side
ArytenoidTriangular pyramids about 15 mm high. The apex articulates with the corniculate cartilage, the concave base with the cricoid lamina. The anterior angle of the base extends as the vocal process (insertion of the vocal ligament); the lateral angle bears the muscular process (insertion of the posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles); the posterior side takes the transverse arytenoid muscle
AccessoryCorniculate: on the apices of the arytenoids. Cuneiform: in the aryepiglottic fold. Others: posterior and anterior sesamoids and interarytenoid

Safety muscles of the larynx. The posterior cricoarytenoids are the only intrinsic muscles that abduct the vocal cords, letting air through the rima glottidis. When they contract, the muscular processes of both arytenoids rotate medially and the vocal processes rotate laterally, giving a wide diamond-shaped opening. If they are paralysed, the adductors take the upper hand and the person might die from lack of air.

Tuning fork of the larynx. The cricothyroid is important for the tone and pitch of the voice: when sound is about to be produced it tenses the cord and makes it ready to vibrate. Paralysis after an external laryngeal nerve lesion alters the voice significantly, especially noticeable in singers.

Nerve damage. External laryngeal nerve: weakness of phonation from loss of the tightening effect of the cricothyroid. Recurrent laryngeal nerve, often damaged accidentally during partial thyroidectomy: unilaterally, the cord lies in the paramedian position and does not vibrate, though the other usually compensates; bilaterally, both cords lie paramedian with loss of phonation and difficulty breathing. If both recurrent and external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides, all the intrinsic muscles are paralysed and the cords are further abducted and fixed: the cadaveric position.

Laryngeal obstruction. The mucosa of the superior larynx is very sensitive, so a foreign body causes immediate explosive coughing. If that reflex is slowed or absent, choking follows. The Heimlich manoeuvre: stand behind the victim, pass your arms under theirs, place your hands in front of the epigastrium with one hand as a fist and the other over it, then give three or four abdominal thrusts directed upwards and backwards, squeezing the residual air up to dislodge the foreign body.

Vocal nodules (singer's or screamer's nodules). The area of maximum contact during vibration is at the junction of the anterior one third and posterior two thirds of the cords, so it takes the most friction. People who overuse the voice develop inflammatory nodules there: bilateral, symmetrical, from pin head to split pea in size, soft, reddish and oedematous early, later greyish or whitish.

The larynx is the upper expanded part of the lower respiratory tract, modified for producing voice, also called the organ of phonation. It is an unpaired median tube of fibro-muscular-cartilaginous constitution: several cartilages linked by joints, muscles and ligaments, lined on their deep surface by a mucous membrane.

It acts as a sphincter at the inlet of the lower respiratory tract, protecting the trachea and bronchial tree from anything other than air. In laryngeal incompetence, food and fluid may be aspirated. Its upward and downward movements also help in swallowing.

Functions: a) phonation, b) respiration, c) protection, d) deglutition.

AspectDetail
SituationThe middle part of the visceral sheath of the neck. Above: the hyoid bone and base of the tongue. Below: the trachea. Behind: the hypopharynx. In front: the thyroid
AgeHigher in children (C2 to C3) than in adults. In newborns it contacts the veil, which is why they keep exclusive nasal breathing until about four months
ExtensionSuperior: the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the body of C4. Inferior: the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage, at the lower edge of C6
Shape and sizeA triangular pyramid with a posterosuperior base (hyoid bone, pharynx) and a lower vertex (trachea). In men: length 4.5 cm, transverse diameter 4 cm, sagittal diameter 3.5 cm. Smaller in women
FixationMobile vertically and transversely, but fixed by its continuity with the pharynx and trachea, and by its union with the hyoid bone and thoracic skeleton through muscles and ligaments

JointDetail
CricoarytenoidThe most important functionally. An elliptical synovial articulation reinforced by the posterior cricoarytenoid ligament, uniting the base of the arytenoid with the upper edge of the cricoid lamina. 1. Rotatory movement around a vertical axis, abducting or adducting the vocal cords. 2. Gliding movement, one arytenoid toward or away from the other, closing or opening the posterior part of the glottis
CricothyroidA flat synovial joint reinforced by ligaments, joining the lower cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the lateral face of the cricoid. Tilting of the cricoid around a transverse axis (arch up, lamina down) tenses the vocal cords

Extrinsic ligaments and membranes attach the cartilages to neighbouring structures and lie outside the inner fibroelastic tube:

  • Thyrohyoid membrane: from the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage to the lower edge of the hyoid bone, with a medial thickening (medial thyroid ligament) and two lateral thickenings (lateral thyroid ligaments).
  • Thyroepiglottic ligament: attaches the lower narrow end of the epiglottis to the posterior surface of the thyroid angle.
  • Hyoepiglottic ligament: connects the posterior aspect of the hyoid with the anterior surface of the upper end of the epiglottis.
  • Cricotracheal ligament: between the lower edge of the cricoid and the upper edge of the first tracheal ring.

Intrinsic ligaments are parts of a broad sheet of fibroelastic tissue forming the inner tube of the laryngeal cavity outside its mucous lining. The cricothyroid ligament, stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process, forms the vocal ligament. The vestibular ligament is tense between the thyroid angle and the anterolateral aspect of the arytenoid.

Intrinsic muscles, by action

  1. Vocal cord tensors: cricothyroid (paired). Action: elevation of the cricoid arch and lowering of the thyroid cartilage, tensing the vocal cord.
  2. Dilator of the glottis: the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only one.
  3. Constrictors of the glottis: lateral cricoarytenoid, interarytenoid, superior thyroarytenoid (from the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage to the lower third of the arytenoid) and inferior thyroarytenoid or vocal muscle (from the reentrant angle to the anterolateral aspect of the arytenoid), which tilts the arytenoid forward and tenses the cord.
FunctionMuscles
Abduct the vocal cordsPosterior cricoarytenoids
Adduct the vocal cordsLateral cricoarytenoids, transverse arytenoid
Tense the vocal cordsCricothyroid, vocalis
Relax the vocal cordsThyroarytenoid

Three exceptions worth memorising. The cricothyroid is the only muscle lying on the outer aspect of the larynx. All the intrinsic muscles are paired except the transverse arytenoid (interarytenoid), which is unpaired. All of them adduct the vocal cords except the posterior cricoarytenoids, which abduct them.

Extrinsic muscles ensure laryngeal mobility, especially during swallowing. Elevators: thyrohyoid, mylohyoid, digastric. Depressors: sternothyroid, sternohyoid, omohyoid.

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
• Describe the components of the larynx and its ways of fixation.
  • Identify cartilages, joints, ligaments and muscles of the larynx and describe their action.
  • Describe innervation, blood supply and lymphatic drainage of the larynx.
  • List the anatomical relations of the larynx.
  • Describe the physiology of phonation.
  • Understand the clinical correlation of larynx anatomy to voice pathology.

The set of mechanisms allowing vibration at the free edge of the vocal fold, transforming aerodynamic energy into acoustic energy. The sound produced is immediately modified and filtered by the supralaryngeal air cavities to become vowels and consonants: the bucco-pharyngeal resonators.

The voice is characterised by three acoustic parameters: frequency, in Hertz, depending on the vibration speed of the vocal folds; intensity, in dB, depending on the force of pulmonary expiration (subglottic pressure); and pitch, depending on the accommodation of the vocal folds but especially on the shape of the supralaryngeal cavities.

Respiratory changes. During phonation the expiratory time lengthens and becomes active, the inspiratory time shortens, the mobilised air volumes are greater and expiratory lung pressures increase. The expiratory blow creates a subglottic pressure that overcomes the resistance of the vocal cords.

The vibratory cycle. 1. Putting into phonatory position: the folds close as the arytenoids come together. 2. Opening: when the subglottic pressure overcomes the muscular and elastic resistance, a puff of air passes at high speed, an acoustic impulse. 3. Closure of the folds.

The supralaryngeal cavities. Filter role: resonance and enrichment of certain frequencies or suppression of others, with two areas of particular enhancement, the pharynx and the oral cavity. The basic laryngeal frequency is enriched with harmonics giving the pitch. Articulation role: through the tongue, pharyngolarynx, jaws, lips and soft palate. Dry or cold ambient air can change the voice through mucous changes in the walls.

Mechanism, step by step. 1. The vocal cords are kept adducted. 2. Infraglottic air pressure is generated by exhaled air from the lungs. 3. The force of air opens the cords and is released as small puffs. 4. Moving air passing through the cords makes them vibrate, producing sound. 5. Sound is amplified by the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus and nose. 6. Sound is converted into speech by the lips, tongue, palate, pharynx and teeth.

Vowels are voiced in the larynx by vibration of the vocal folds; consonants are produced by the intrinsic muscles of the tongue. Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration, pitch on the frequency. Male cords are usually longer, so they vibrate with greater amplitude but lower frequency: louder but lower pitched.

CompartmentContents
SupraglotticVestibule: a pyramidal space from the laryngeal margin to the ventricular bands. Laryngeal or Morgagni ventricle: between the ventricular bands (false vocal cords) above and the plane of the vocal cords below. This is the ENT surgeon's view of the nose, and it is built around one idea: the nasal cavity is a crossroads. Its roof is the skull base, its lateral walls touch the orbits, its floor is the palate, and every paranasal sinus drains into it.

Two things follow, and both are exam favourites. The rich blood supply from both carotid systems explains epistaxis. The drainage sites on the lateral wall explain sinusitis.

Rhinitis. Inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the nasal cavity. Hypertrophy of the mucosa over the inferior concha is a common feature of allergic rhinitis. It presents as nasal blockage, sneezing and watery discharge from the nose (rhinorrhea). Excessive rhinorrhea due to vasomotor and allergic rhinitis can be controlled by sectioning the Vidian nerve.

Little's area. An area in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule. It is highly vascular: the septal branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose there to form Kiesselbach's plexus. This is the commonest site of epistaxis in children and young adults, usually due to fingernail trauma from picking the nose.

Sinusitis. Infection of a paranasal air sinus, presenting as headache and persistent thick purulent discharge from the nose. On standard radiological images normal sinuses are radiolucent, whereas diseased sinuses show varying degrees of opacity. CT gives very clear images that significantly aid diagnosis.

Two narrow cavities separated by a thin sagittal wall, located in the centre of the facial bones, in front of the rhinopharynx, above the oral cavity, below the skull base and between the orbits. They communicate with the outside through the nostrils and open back into the rhinopharynx via the choanae. The two cavities are often asymmetric, given the frequency of septal deviations.

  • Framework: osteo-cartilaginous, cartilaginous in front and bony behind.
  • Lining: pituitary mucosa, respiratory.
  • Shape: two long sagittal corridors.
  • Four walls: roof, floor, medial and lateral. Two apertures: anterior and posterior.

Anterior opening: the bony piriform aperture, circumscribed above by the nasal bones and below and laterally by the frontal process of the maxillary bone. More anteriorly is the vestibule, with the major alar cartilage and the septal cartilage.

External nose. A pyramidal projection in the mid face: 1. the tip (apex), the lower free end. 2. the root or bridge, the upper narrow part continuous with the forehead. 3. the dorsum, a round border between tip and root where the sides meet. 4. the nostrils or nares, the two piriform apertures at the broad lower end. 5. the ala, the lower flared part on the side.

Posterior orifice, the choana. Oval with a large vertical axis, limited above by the body of the sphenoid, below by the horizontal plate of the palate, laterally by the pterygoid process, and medially by the vomer, which separates the two choanae.

• The nose and nasal cavities are formed by five facial prominences derived from the first branchial arch, appearing at the end of the fifth week.
  • The nasal cavities derive from the nasal placodes, which invaginate to form the primitive nasal cavity, the primitive olfactory gutter.
  • Initially the oronasal membrane separates the nasal cavity from the primary oral cavity.
  • The nasal cavity is separated from the oral cavity by the maturation of the primary and secondary palate.
  • The paranasal sinuses develop from diverticula in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
1. Know the descriptive anatomy of the nasal cavity.
  2. Describe the components of the nasal cavity walls.
  3. Explain the rich blood supply of the nasal cavity.
  4. Name the relations of the nasal cavity.
  5. Explain nasal physiology.

The nose is the uppermost part of the respiratory tract and contains the peripheral organ of smell. It consists of the external nose and the nasal cavity. The Greek word for nose is rhinos, so the study of the nose and its diseases is termed rhinology.

Functions: 1. Respiration. 2. Olfaction. 3. Protection of the lower respiratory passages. 4. Air conditioning of the inspired air. 5. Vocal resonance. 6. Nasal reflex functions, for example sneezing.

Three domains: ventilation, immunity and olfaction.

Ventilatory function. Four roles: 1. airflow control (rheostat). 2. filtration. 3. humidification (hygrostat). 4. heating (thermostat).

  • Regulation of airflow. Inspired air meets obstacles in the nasal corridor, creating resistance and turning laminar flow into turbulent flow. Three valves modify the size of the nasal fossa: the nostril valve, the nasal valve and the septo-turbinal valve.
  • Filtration. The role of mucus, its adhesiveness, the mucociliary movement and the slope of the nasal floor and meatus. Contaminated mucus is evacuated and swallowed.
  • Humidification. Contact and exchange between the inspired air and the mucus layer.
  • Warming. About 70 percent happens in the nasal cavity, by slowing the flow and through local heat from the mucous surface and the conchae.

Immune function. Three lines of defence: non-specific inflammation, the epithelial line, and the specific line, NALT and IgA.

Physiology of the ostia. They ensure sinus ventilation (gas diffusion) and sinus drainage (mucociliary function). Ostium obstruction leads to transudate and exudate, ciliary slowdown, hypoxia, oedema and rhinosinusitis.

Both the internal and external carotid systems contribute, which is why the nose bleeds so readily.

Venous drainage. Two networks, a deep periosteal one and a superficial mucous one, draining to the internal maxillary vein, the ophthalmic vein and the facial vein.

Innervation: rich. By branches of V and I. Sensory nerves (V): the spheno-palatine nerve (V2) and the internal nasal nerve. Olfactory nerves (I): a yellowish pigmented zone on the convex face of the upper concha and the upper part of the septum, and a sensory area, the olfactory spot, containing the olfactory cells.

The neck is mapped in triangles because a surgeon needs constant landmarks in a small space crowded with vital structures. Learn the two big triangles first, then their subdivisions, then the four small ones this paper is really about.

The key: sternocleidomastoid splits the neck in two. Everything in front of it is the anterior triangle, everything behind it the posterior triangle.

Why they matter. These triangles are reliable and constant landmarks for head and neck surgeons: for identifying the common carotid artery, ligating the lingual artery, identifying the hypoglossal nerve, and recognising the common facial vein.

The neck connects the head with the rest of the body and is the most mobile part of the trunk. It is cylindrical, of constant length but uneven diameter. The well-known landmarks are the thyroid cartilage, the hyoid bone, the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Bordered superiorly by the inferior border of the body of the mandible, lying between the anterior and posterior bellies of digastric. It is subdivided into anterior and posterior parts by the stylomandibular ligament.

Beclard's, Lesser's and Pirogoff's triangles, the forgotten or smaller triangles of the neck, are housed within the submandibular triangle.

The nervous system is the most complex organ system of the body. It is studied in two parts: the central nervous system (CNS), the command centre, and the peripheral nervous system (PNS), the communication network linking the CNS to muscles, glands and sensory organs.

This framework is what lets a doctor localise a lesion from the symptoms and plan a neurosurgical approach.

The whole nervous system comes from ectoderm: neural plate, then neural groove, then neural tube. The tube's cranial end swells into 3 primary then 5 secondary vesicles, which become the parts of the adult brain, and its lumen becomes the ventricular system.

• The general organisation of the nervous system: CNS and PNS, somatic and autonomic.
  • The cellular basis of nervous tissue: neurons, glial cells, grey and white matter.
  • The embryology of the nervous system: neural tube, primary and secondary vesicles, flexures, neural tube defects.

Learning objectives: understand CNS and PNS organisation, relate structure to function, and explain clinical localisation and neurosurgical approaches.
Three steps: sensory input (receptors detect a stimulus), integration (the brain and spinal cord process and interpret it) and motor output (effector muscles and glands respond).

• Two major components: the brain (cerebrum, brainstem, cerebellum) and the spinal cord.
  • Protected by bone (skull and vertebral column), reinforced by the meninges and cushioned by CSF, because it controls vital functions.

All neural elements outside the CNS, connecting it to organs, limbs and skin.

  • 12 pairs of cranial nerves, arising from the brain.
  • 31 pairs of spinal nerves, arising from the spinal cord.
  • Peripheral ganglia: collections of nerve cell bodies outside the CNS: sensory (dorsal root ganglia) and autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic).

Functional divisions: the somatic system controls voluntary actions; the autonomic system responds automatically, with a sympathetic (fight or flight) and a parasympathetic (rest and digest) division.

The neuron is the basic structural and functional unit, specialised for communication: cell body (soma) with the nucleus, dendrites that receive signals, an axon that carries impulses away from the soma, and axon terminals that release neurotransmitters.

Glial cells are more numerous than neurons; they do not transmit impulses but are essential.

Two halves. First the vessels: one artery, the ophthalmic, supplies almost everything in the orbit, and the ophthalmic veins carry it all back to the cavernous sinus. Second the clinic: what goes wrong, and why the anatomy explains it.

The clinical half is the payoff for the whole module. A drooping lid, a squint, a blown pupil, a lost corneal reflex: each one points back to a specific nerve or muscle you have already learned.

title: Disorders of eye movement and refraction
subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
Strabismus (squint). The eyes don't point in the same direction. It is caused by nerve damage or problems in the eye muscles: when some muscles around the eye are weaker than others they cannot work together, so one eye looks at one object while the other turns in a different direction. The most common type is one eye turning slightly inwards, towards the nose. One eye may turn inwards, outwards, upwards or downwards while the other looks forward. Squints affect about one in 20 children.

TypeDirection
EsotropiaInward turning
ExotropiaOutward turning
HypotropiaDownward turning
HypertropiaUpward turning

Nystagmus. A vision condition in which the eyes make repetitive, uncontrolled movements, often resulting in reduced vision and depth perception, and affecting balance and coordination. The movements can be horizontal, vertical or rotary. It is caused by a miscommunication between the eye and the brain, affecting the way the brain interprets movement signals; it is typically caused by brain injuries and results from brain damage. It is sometimes called dancing eyes.

Myopia and hyperopia. A nearsighted (myopic) person sees near objects clearly while distant objects are blurred. Farsightedness (hyperopia) is the visual image being focused behind the retina rather than directly on it; it may be caused by the eyeball being too small or the focusing power being too weak.

Direct and consensual pupillary light reflex. A direct pupillary reflex is the response of a pupil to light that enters the ipsilateral (same) eye. A consensual reflex is the response of a pupil to light that enters the contralateral (opposite) eye.

Loss of the corneal reflex. Absence may indicate deep coma or stroke, either unilaterally or bilaterally. Unilateral loss may also indicate a lesion involving the trigeminal or facial nerve. Repeat the test on the patient's other eye, and document the reflex as present or absent, unilateral or bilateral.

A pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasma produces bitemporal hemianopia, because the crossing nasal fibres carry the temporal halves of both visual fields.

Which cells continue as the optic nerve? The ganglion cells: their axons leave the eye at the optic disc.

Blowout fractures are classified by the perimeter of the orbit they affect. The most common are those of the inferior orbital wall, the floor.

  • In approximately half of cases they occur in unison with fractures affecting the medial orbital wall.
  • The majority of orbital floor fractures occur in the posteromedial portion of the bone, in relation to the infraorbital groove.
  • With orbital floor fractures, prolapse of orbital fat into the maxillary sinus may be seen, sometimes accompanied by inferior rectus muscle prolapse.
  • Following inferior blowout fractures, the second commonest is that of the medial wall, with prolapse of the medial rectus muscle and orbital fat into the air cells of the ethmoid.
  • Fractures to the superior border of the orbit are rare, and those to the lateral walls are even rarer, because that border is fortified with thicker bone and more muscle. Lateral fractures are seen in very severe accidents with extensive injury to the craniofacial area.
  • Superior blowout fractures may involve the neighbouring sinus as well as the anterior cranial fossa, presenting with leakage of cerebrospinal fluid.

Corneal abrasion is generally the result of trauma to the surface of the eye: a fingernail scratching the eye, walking into something, or getting grit in the eye, particularly if it is rubbed. It can also be caused by contact lens insertion and removal. Most heal within a few days and cause no further problems; those that don't heal or don't respond to treatment could lead to infections or scarring, and both can cause loss of vision.

From eye to cortex, in order:

  1. Eye (retina)
  2. Optic nerve
  3. Optic chiasm: the fibres from the medial (nasal) half of each retina cross over to the optic tract of the opposite side
  4. Optic tract
  5. Lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay centre in the thalamus, where the ganglion fibres synapse
  6. Optic radiation
  7. Primary visual cortex, in the occipital lobe

Cortical areas shown in the lecture: primary visual cortex, secondary visual cortex, inferotemporal area and posterior parietal area.

Where damage occurs, and what is lost

SiteWhereVisual loss
1Left optic nerve, cutTotal loss of vision from the left eye
2Left optic nerve, partialInformation from the nasal visual field of the left eye (the temporal part of the left retina) is lost
3Optic chiasmThe temporal (lateral) portions of the visual field are lost in both eyes: the crossing fibres are cut
4 and 5Optic tract, or the fibre tract from the lateral geniculate to the cortexIdentical visual loss in both eyes: in this example, loss of vision of the right side

Partial damage to these fibre tracts causes other predictable visual problems.

The circuitry that changes the diameter of the pupil when there is sufficient light. It includes bilateral projections from the retina to the pretectum and projections from the pretectum to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. Neurons in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel in cranial nerve III to the ciliary ganglion, and neurons in the ciliary ganglion innervate the pupillary constrictor muscle.

Because the afferent axons activate both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, light shone in one eye constricts both pupils.

Visual retina. Neural layer: light-receptive, ending anteriorly along the ora serrata. Pigmented cell layer: a single layer of cells that absorbs light to reduce scattering within the eye.

Non-visual retina. The portion of the retina that is not sensitive to light: the anterior continuation of the pigment cell layer plus supporting cells over the ciliary body and posterior surface of the iris.

LandmarkNote
Optic disc (papilla)The blind spot: no photoreceptors. In the fundus of the retina, where the sensory fibres of the optic nerve enter the eyeball
MaculaSpecial photoreceptor cones for visual acuity; lacks blood vessels
FoveaAt the centre of the macula; high-acuity vision; densely saturated with cone photoreceptors

Signalling. Photoreceptors and bipolar cells produce graded potentials rather than action potentials. Ganglion cells generate action potentials, and their axons join together to form the optic nerve, which exits through the back of the eye at the optic disc. Note that light travels in the opposite direction to the flow of neuronal communication.

The mouth is a box with a bony roof, a muscular floor and a muscular organ in the middle. Learn its two compartments first, the vestibule outside the teeth and the oral cavity proper inside, then hang everything else on that.

The tongue carries the heaviest nerve load in the body for its size: four different cranial nerves for sensation and taste, plus CN XII for movement. That list is the single most tested thing here.

Extends from the lips to the oropharyngeal isthmus, the junction of mouth and pharynx, bounded above by the soft palate and the palatoglossal folds, and below by the dorsum of the tongue. It is subdivided into the vestibule and the oral cavity proper.

PartDescription
VestibuleA slit-like space between the cheeks and the gums, communicating with the exterior through the oral fissure. When the jaws are closed it communicates with the oral cavity proper behind the third molar tooth on each side. Limited above and below by the reflection of mucous membrane from lips and cheek onto the gums. Its lateral wall is the cheek, formed by the buccinator, covered laterally by skin and medially by mucous membrane. A small papilla opposite the upper second molar marks the opening of the parotid duct.
Oral cavity properThe cavity within the alveolar margins of the maxillae and the mandible. Roof: the hard palate anteriorly and the soft palate posteriorly. Floor: the mylohyoid muscle, with the anterior two thirds of the tongue lying on it.

Floor of the mouth. Covered with mucous membrane. In the midline, a mucosal fold, the frenulum, connects the tongue to the floor. On each side of the frenulum, a small papilla carries the opening of the submandibular duct. A rounded ridge extending backward and laterally from the papilla is produced by the sublingual gland.

Three major glands: the parotid, submandibular and sublingual.

Parotid gland

Para = around, otic = ear. The largest major salivary gland, purely serous, weighing about 15 grams. Its superficial portion lies in front of the external ear, and its deeper part fills the retromolar fossa.

  • Arteries: external carotid, maxillary, superficial temporal, posterior auricular.
  • Veins: the retromandibular vein is formed within the gland by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.
  • Nerves: the facial nerve enters the gland and divides into its terminal branches within it.
  • Duct: Stensen's duct crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator to open at a papilla on the buccal mucosa opposite the maxillary second molar. It measures 4 to 6 mm in length and 5 mm in diameter. A small portion of the parotid accompanies the duct, forming the accessory gland.

Submandibular gland

The second largest, also called the submaxillary salivary gland. A mixed gland with both serous and mucous units, but serous units predominate. Its superficial part fills the digastric triangle; its deep part lies deep to the mylohyoid and superficial to the hyoglossus and styloglossus. Its duct, Wharton's duct, runs forward above the mylohyoid muscle just below the mucosa and the floor of the mouth, and opens on the sublingual papilla (caruncula sublingualis), lateral to the lingual frenulum.

Sublingual gland

The smallest of the major salivary glands. It lies between the floor of the mouth, below the mucosa and above the mylohyoid muscle. A mixed gland, but mucous units predominate. Its duct opens near the submandibular duct, and several small ducts, the ducts of Rivinus, open independently along the sublingual fold.

The palate lies in the roof of the oral cavity and has two parts: the hard (bony) palate anteriorly and the soft (muscular) palate posteriorly.

Hard palate. Lies in the roof of the oral cavity and forms the floor of the nasal cavity. Formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind, bounded by the alveolar arches.

Soft palate. Attached to the posterior border of the hard palate, covered on its upper and lower surfaces by mucous membrane. Composed of muscle fibres, an aponeurosis, lymphoid tissue, glands, blood vessels and nerves.

Palatine aponeurosis. A fibrous sheath attached to the posterior border of the hard palate. It is the expanded tendon of tensor veli palatini, splits to enclose the musculus uvulae, and gives origin and insertion to the palatine muscles.

A mass of striated muscles covered with mucous membrane, divided into right and left halves by a median septum. Three parts: oral (anterior two thirds), pharyngeal (posterior third) and root. Two surfaces: dorsal and ventral.

Dorsal surface. Divided into anterior two thirds and posterior one third by a V-shaped sulcus terminalis. The apex of the sulcus faces backward and is marked by a pit, the foramen cecum, an embryological remnant marking the site of the upper end of the thyroglossal duct. The anterior two thirds are rough with three types of papillae: filiform, fungiform and vallate. The posterior third has no papillae but a nodular surface from underlying lymphatic nodules, the lingual tonsils.

Ventral surface. Smooth, with no papillae. The frenulum connects the tongue to the floor of the mouth in the midline. Lateral to it the deep lingual vein can be seen through the mucosa, and lateral to that a fold of mucosa forms the plica fimbriata.

Motor: the hypoglossal nerve supplies all the muscles; the vagus nerve supplies the palatoglossus.

Blood: lingual artery, tonsillar branch of the facial artery, ascending pharyngeal artery. Veins: the lingual vein, draining into the internal jugular vein.

Lymph: tip to the submental nodes bilaterally then deep cervical; anterior two thirds to the submandibular nodes unilaterally then deep cervical; posterior third to the deep cervical nodes, mainly the jugulodigastric.

Functions. The most important articulator for speech production. Its primary function is to provide a mechanism for taste: taste buds are on different areas of the tongue but generally found around the edges, sensitive to four main tastes: bitter, sour, salty and sweet.

The orbit is a bony, pyramid-shaped socket that protects the eyeball and holds the muscles, nerves and vessels that serve it. Its base opens onto the face. Its apex points back and inward, toward the middle of the skull.

The eyeball is the star of the orbit, but it cannot work alone. This lecture is about everything around it: the eyelids that protect and clean it, the tear film that keeps it wet, the lacrimal gland that makes the tears, and the nerves that turn that gland on and off.

One theme runs through it all: keeping the cornea covered in fluid. Blinking spreads it, glands supply it, and the nasolacrimal system drains it away.

• The eyeball, the most essential content

The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid and is supplied by the oculomotor nerve. Its deeper smooth muscle part, the superior tarsal muscle, is supplied by sympathetic fibres.

The eyelid is 2 to 3 mm thick and has a medial part and a lateral part. The lateral part carries the eyelashes and is known as the ciliary part.

Orbicularis oculi. Its orbital part is anchored by the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments.

Conjunctiva. It keeps the surface of the eye and the eyelids lubricated and protects the ocular surface from microbial infection. The palpebral conjunctiva reflects at the superior and inferior conjunctival fornices onto the eyeball as the bulbar conjunctiva, enclosing the conjunctival sac.

1. Parasympathetic stimulation reaches the gland.

Structure. About 2 cm long, in two parts: the orbital part (larger, on the lateral margin of the levator palpebrae superioris) and the palpebral part (smaller, along the inner surface of the eyelid). The pharynx is where the airway and the food way cross. A funnel of muscle from the skull base to the oesophagus, it has to route air forward into the larynx and food backward into the oesophagus without ever mixing them up.

Two things carry the lecture: the three subdivisions and what sits in each, and the swallowing sequence, which is the anatomy in motion.

The pharynx is a funnel-shaped fibromuscular tube extending from the base of the skull to the oesophagus, lined throughout with mucous membrane. It acts as a common channel for both food (deglutition) and air (respiration), contains the tonsils of Waldeyer's ring, and carries the connection to the middle ear.

Measurements: length 12 to 14 cm; width 3.5 cm at its base and 1.5 cm at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction. It lies behind the cavities of the nose, mouth and larynx, with which it communicates.

Piriform fossa. A deep recess, broad above and narrow below, in the anterior part of the lateral wall of the laryngopharynx on each side of the laryngeal inlet, produced by the bulging of the larynx into the laryngopharynx. Swallowed foreign bodies may lodge there.

The process by which food is transferred from the mouth to the stomach, in three successive stages.

First stage, in the mouth: voluntary. The mouth is closed and the anterior part of the tongue is raised against the hard palate in front of the bolus, pushing the masticated food progressively into the posterior part of the oral cavity. The soft palate closes down onto the back of the tongue to help form the bolus. The hyoid bone moves up and food is pushed from the oral cavity into the oropharynx through the oropharyngeal isthmus.

Second stage, in the pharynx: involuntary and very rapid. The nasopharyngeal isthmus is closed by elevation of the soft palate and contraction of Passavant's ridge, preventing entry of food into the nasopharynx. The laryngeal inlet is closed by approximation of the aryepiglottic folds. The pharynx and larynx are elevated behind the hyoid bone by the longitudinal muscles, and the bolus is pushed down over the posterior surface of the epiglottis by gravity and contraction of the superior and middle constrictors, passing from oropharynx to laryngopharynx. Rapid downward displacement of the larynx and pharynx by the infrahyoid muscles then reopens the laryngeal orifice.

Third stage, in the oesophagus: involuntary. The propulsive action of thyropharyngeus, followed by relaxation of cricopharyngeus, pushes the food from the laryngopharynx into the oesophagus, and peristaltic movements of the oesophageal wall carry it to the stomach.

EffectsFight or flight: faster heart, mydriasis, bronchodilation, reduced gut activity, sweating, skin and gut vasoconstriction, glucose releaseRest and digest: slower heart, miosis, salivation and lacrimation, gut motility, bladder contraction, erection

Enteric nervous system: sometimes a third division; the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus controls motility and the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus secretion and blood flow.

Central control: the hypothalamus (main integrator), brainstem nuclei (cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes), spinal cord (visceral reflexes) and limbic cortex (emotional responses).

Clinical: diabetic autonomic neuropathy (orthostatic hypotension, bladder dysfunction, impotence); Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis); vasovagal syncope; Raynaud's disease.

The peripheral nervous system is everything outside the brain and spinal cord: 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves, with their plexuses and ganglia.

Two ways to split it. Anatomically: cranial versus spinal. Functionally: somatic (voluntary, one neuron to muscle) versus autonomic (involuntary, two neurons, sympathetic and parasympathetic).

NerveTypeFunction
I OlfactorySensorySmell
II OpticSensoryVision
III OculomotorMotorEye movement, lid elevation, pupillary constriction
IV TrochlearMotorEye movement (superior oblique)
VI AbducensMotorEye movement (lateral rectus)
V TrigeminalMixedFacial sensation, muscles of mastication
VII FacialMixedFacial expression, part of taste, saliva
VIII VestibulocochlearSensoryHearing and balance
IX GlossopharyngealMixedMuscles of mouth and upper throat, part of taste, saliva
X VagusMixedHomeostatic control of thoracic and upper abdominal organs
XI AccessoryMotorNeck muscles, with cervical spinal nerves
XII HypoglossalMotorTongue and lower throat muscles

Autonomic fibres: III (pupillary constriction), VII and IX (salivation), X (thoracic and upper abdominal ganglia).

Olfactory nerve. Bipolar neurons of the olfactory epithelium send axons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulbs, then along the olfactory tracts to the olfactory cortex, amygdala and hypothalamus.

Visual pathway. Retina, optic nerve of ganglion cell axons (wrapped in meninges, through the optic canal), optic chiasm above the pituitary where nasal fibres cross, optic tract carrying the contralateral field of both eyes, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, and the primary visual cortex, V1 or area 17, around the calcarine sulcus. Some tract fibres go to the superior colliculus, pretectal area and hypothalamus.

LesionDefect
Optic nerveIpsilateral blindness
Optic chiasmBitemporal hemianopia
Optic tractContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Occipital cortexContralateral homonymous hemianopia, with macular sparing after a PCA stroke

CN III, IV and VI. III from the midbrain, through the cavernous sinus, to the superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris. IV from the dorsal midbrain to the superior oblique. VI from the pons, through the cavernous sinus, to the lateral rectus.

Trigeminal nerve. The largest cranial nerve, with a large sensory and small motor root from the pons; sensory fibres synapse in the Gasserian ganglion in Meckel's cave. Ophthalmic (sensory) via the superior orbital fissure; maxillary (sensory) via the foramen rotundum; mandibular (sensory and motor) via the foramen ovale.

Facial nerve. The motor pathway runs from the inferior precentral gyrus through the genu of the internal capsule to the facial nucleus. The upper face receives bilateral input, the lower face only contralateral. The nerve enters the internal auditory canal with CN VIII, then crosses the temporal bone in three segments: labyrinthine (narrowest, to the geniculate ganglion), tympanic (above the oval window) and mastoid (giving the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani). It exits by the stylomastoid foramen, enters the parotid and divides into five purely motor branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical.

The PNS is the communication link between the CNS and the body, carrying sensation to the CNS and motor commands to muscles and glands. Anatomically it is the cranial nerves, spinal nerves and their branches, plexuses and ganglia. Functionally it is the somatic system (voluntary movement and conscious sensation) and the autonomic system (involuntary visceral control).

Histology. Axons run in bundles called fibres; multiple fibres form a nerve, with connective tissue and blood vessels. Afferent nerves carry information to the CNS; efferent nerves carry commands from it.

Voluntary movement through skeletal muscle, plus sensation from skin, muscles and joints.

  • Sensory division: touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain and proprioception; cell bodies in dorsal root or cranial sensory ganglia.
  • Motor division: a single neuron from the ventral horn or a cranial motor nucleus straight to the muscle, with no ganglion, releasing acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors.

Reflex arc: 1. receptor, 2. sensory neuron, 3. integration centre in the cord, 4. motor neuron, 5. effector muscle. The patellar reflex is monosynaptic and tests spinal segment integrity.

Every spinal nerve carries combined sensory and motor axons in two roots: sensory axons enter as the dorsal root, motor fibres leave as the ventral root. The dorsal root ganglion is an enlargement of the nerve. 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal, each leaving through its intervertebral foramen.

PlexusRootsMain nerves
CervicalC1 to C5Posterior neck and head; the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm
BrachialC4 to T1Radial, axillary, ulnar, median
LumbarLumbarPelvis and anterior leg; the femoral nerve and its saphenous branch
SacralL4 to S4The sciatic nerve (tibial plus fibular)

The sciatic nerve is the largest and longest in the body, from L4 to S3. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below piriformis, descends deep to gluteus maximus and down the posterior thigh on adductor magnus, supplying the hamstrings. Near the popliteal fossa it divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves. Sciatica is most commonly caused by a bulging or herniated disc.

Four air-filled sinuses sit in the bones around the nose, and every one of them drains back into the nasal cavity. If you learn nothing else, learn where each one opens, because that single fact explains sinusitis, why infection spreads, and half the exam questions.

The shortcut: the middle meatus is the busy one. Maxillary, frontal and the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells all drain there.

Frontal sinuses

  • One on each side. Variable in size and the most superior of the sinuses, averaging 2.5 cm. Each is triangular in shape.
  • Rudimentary at birth and usually well developed by the age of 7 or 8.
  • Drains onto the lateral wall of the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct.
  • Nerves: branches of the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves from the ophthalmic nerve (V1). Blood: branches of the anterior ethmoidal, supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries.

Ethmoidal sinus

  • Composed of three sets of ethmoidal air cells: anterior, middle and posterior, with 3 to 18 cells on each side.
  • The thin-walled, bony, honeycombed spaces collectively form the ethmoidal labyrinth, between the orbits and the nasal fossae. It may invade any of the other three sinuses.
  • Ethmoid bulla: the middle ethmoid air cells produce this swelling on the lateral wall of the middle meatus.
  • Nerves: the anterior and posterior ethmoidal branches of the nasociliary nerve (V1), and the maxillary nerve (V2) via orbital branches from the pterygopalatine ganglion. Blood: branches of the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries. Lymph: submandibular nodes (anterior and middle cells), retropharyngeal nodes (posterior cells).

Maxillary sinuses

  • One on each side, the largest of the paranasal sinuses, about 3.5 x 2.5 x 3.5 cm. It completely fills the body of the maxilla and is pyramidal in shape.
  • Roof: the inferior orbital margin. Floor: the alveolus of the maxilla. Base: the lateral wall of the nose. Apex: the zygomatic process of the maxilla.
  • Nerves: the infraorbital and alveolar branches of the maxillary nerve (V2). Blood: branches from the infraorbital and superior alveolar branches of the maxillary arteries. Lymph: the submandibular nodes.

Sphenoidal sinuses

  • Two large, irregularly shaped cavities separated by a septum.
  • Superior: the hypophyseal fossa, pituitary gland and optic chiasma. Inferior: the nasopharynx and pterygoid canal. Medial: the other sphenoid bone. Lateral: the cavernous sinus, internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.
  • Nerves: a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1) and the maxillary nerve (V2). Blood: branches of the pharyngeal arteries from the maxillary arteries.

• The uppermost parts of the respiratory tract, containing the olfactory receptors.
  • Elongated wedge-shaped spaces with a large inferior base and a narrow superior apex.
  • The skeletal framework consists mainly of bone and cartilage.
  • Nares: the external opening of the nose. Choanae: open into the nasopharynx.

External nose. Nasal bone, frontal process of the maxilla, lateral process of the septal cartilage, superior margin of the septal cartilage, major alar cartilage and minor alar cartilages, with the lacrimal bone and nasolacrimal groove behind.

Lateral wall. The conchae divide each nasal cavity into four air channels:

ChannelWhere it lies
Inferior nasal meatusBetween the inferior concha and the nasal floor
Middle nasal meatusBetween the inferior and middle conchae
Superior nasal meatusBetween the middle and superior conchae
Spheno-ethmoidal recessBetween the superior concha and the nasal roof

SinusOpeningLocationConstancy
MaxillaryMaxillary ostiumMiddle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulumConstant
MaxillaryAccessory maxillary ostiumMiddle meatusInconstant
FrontalFrontonasal duct, frontal ostiumFrontal recess of the middle meatusConstant
FrontalMiddle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulumInconstant
Ethmoidal, posterior cellsOstia of the posterior ethmoidal air cellsSuperior meatusConstant
Ethmoidal, middle cellsOstia of the middle ethmoidal air cellsMiddle meatusConstant
Ethmoidal, anterior cellsOstia of the anterior ethmoidal air cellsMiddle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulum, or via the frontal recessInconstant
SphenoidalSphenoidal ostiumSpheno-ethmoidal recessConstant

Invaginations from the nasal cavity that drain into spaces associated with the lateral nasal wall. There are four paranasal air sinuses: the ethmoidal cells, sphenoidal, maxillary and frontal sinuses.

Functions: they make the skull lighter and add resonance to the voice. Infection causes sinusitis.

Development: rudimentary or even absent at birth; enlarge rapidly at the age of 6 to 7 years, then again after puberty. They increase in size through enlargement of the bones from birth to adult life, and resorption of bone in old age. All are lined by respiratory epithelium.

The spinal cord is a cable and a computer at once: it carries messages between brain and body, and it runs reflexes on its own. In cross-section the rule is simple: grey matter inside, shaped like a butterfly, white matter outside, and sensory at the back, motor at the front.

The single most tested fact: in adults the cord ends at L1/L2, which is why lumbar puncture is done lower down.

The caudal end of the neural tube forms the spinal cord. Its wall organises into three layers:

ZonePositionBecomes
Ventricular (ependymal)InnermostNeuroblasts and glioblasts
MantleMiddleGrey matter
MarginalOutermostWhite matter

The mantle layer splits into the dorsal alar plate (sensory) and the ventral basal plate (motor), separated by the sulcus limitans, with autonomic neurons in the intermediate zone. Ventral roots come from basal plate motor neurons; dorsal roots come from neural crest cells.

Ascent of the cord. The cord stops growing at about 4, the spine at 14 to 18. So the cord's end reaches S1 at 6 fetal months, L3 at birth and the L1/L2 disc in adults, occupying the upper two thirds of the canal. This explains the oblique lower roots, the cauda equina.

Cylindrical, flattened anteroposteriorly; cervical curvature concave posteriorly, thoracic concave anteriorly. Length 40 to 45 cm, transverse diameter 10 to 12 mm, anteroposterior about 8 mm, mass 25 to 30 g.

It runs from the foramen magnum to the lower border of L1, ending as the conus medullaris. The filum terminale runs from the conus to the first coccygeal vertebra, anchoring it. It has two enlargements. Each segment, a myelomere, corresponds to a pair of spinal nerves: 31 pairs (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal).

PartExtent and role
CervicalMedulla to C7; cervical enlargement C4 to T1 for the upper limbs
ThoracicT1 to T12; narrower, less grey matter
LumbarT12 to L1/L2; lumbar enlargement L1 to S3 for the lower limbs
SacralBeyond the lumbar enlargement; pelvis and lower limbs
Conus medullarisTapered end at L1 to L2 in adults
Cauda equinaLower roots below the conus, in the lumbar cistern
Filum terminaleFibrous anchor to the coccyx

Surface grooves: a deep anterior median fissure, a shallow posterior median sulcus, and anterolateral and posterolateral sulci where the root filaments emerge.

Main functions: conduction; reflex activity independent of the brain, such as the withdrawal reflex; and autonomic control. The cord also modifies and integrates the information passing through it.

Reflex arc. Spinal reflexes are monosynaptic or polysynaptic.

Segmental organization. Each segment supplies a dermatome (skin) and a myotome (muscles).

Spinal cord compression is a neurosurgical emergency, with a localized lesion syndrome, a sublesional syndrome and a spinal syndrome, assessed with MRI and CT.

Your professor's review questions: the adult cord ends at L1/L2; the intervertebral foramina transmit spinal nerves; the grey matter gives the butterfly appearance; proprioception travels mainly in the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway; the epidural space holds fat and the venous plexus; and lumbar puncture is done below L3 because the cord has ended above.

Grey matter: central, butterfly or H-shaped, with four horns.

HornRole
Posterior (dorsal)Receives sensory input from the dorsal roots
Anterior (ventral)Motor neurons to muscles via the ventral roots: a lateral group for the limbs, a medial group for trunk, head and neck
LateralT1 to L2 for sympathetic outflow; S2 to S4 for parasympathetic outflow

White matter: peripheral, myelinated axons in tracts, divided on each side into anterior, lateral and posterior funiculi. Ascending: dorsal columns (fine touch, proprioception) and spinothalamic tracts (pain, temperature). Descending: corticospinal (voluntary movement) and vestibulospinal (balance, posture).

Spinal nerves. Formed by a sensory root from the back and a motor root from the front, with the dorsal root ganglion holding the sensory cell bodies. Below the conus the roots turn vertical as the cauda equina, which protects the cord from a lumbar puncture needle.

body.html:
1. Describe the gross and microscopic anatomy of the spinal cord.
  2. Explain its embryological development.
  3. Identify its functional organization.
  4. Apply anatomical knowledge to clinical cases.

The spinal cord is the caudal part of the central nervous system, extending down from the brainstem through the vertebral column: both a nervous centre and a conduit for ascending and descending pathways.

Spinal canal. Anteriorly the vertebral bodies, discs and longitudinal ligaments; posteriorly the laminae; laterally the pedicles, which delimit the intervertebral foramina for the spinal nerves. Diameter 12 to 22 mm cervical, 22 to 25 mm lumbar. It contains the cord, meninges, vessels, roots and fatty tissue.

Meninges, outside in: dura (periosteal and meningeal layers), arachnoid and pia. The subarachnoid space holds CSF. The pia sends the denticulate ligament laterally to the dura. The meninges follow the roots to the foramina as nerve sheaths. Fat and the venous plexus lie in the epidural space.

Arteries. The vertebral artery gives the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; segmental arteries (deep cervical, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal) give 31 pairs of radicular branches. Veins run to radicular veins, the vertebral venous plexus, then the vertebral and segmental veins.

The thyroid is an endocrine gland wrapped around the top of the trachea. The anatomy matters because thyroid surgery is common, and two neighbours make it dangerous: the recurrent laryngeal nerves and the parathyroid glands.

Two facts to hold onto: the gland is tied to the larynx and trachea by the ligaments of Berry, which is why a thyroid lump moves when you swallow; and its venous plexus lies deep to the true capsule, which is why the capsule comes out with the gland.

Two vertical lateral lobes joined by a horizontal transverse isthmus. Seen from the front the whole looks roughly like an H, or a butterfly, moulded on the aerodigestive axis.

MeasureValue
Height of the lateral lobes6 cm
Width between lateral edges6 cm
Isthmus1 cm wide by 1.5 cm high
WeightAbout 30 g, variable; bigger in women than in men

Each lateral lobe is a triangular pyramid with a tapered apex (upper pole) resting against the posterior and inferior part of the thyroid cartilage, a rounded base (lower pole) one or two centimetres from the sternum, and three sides: a peripheral (anterolateral) convex superficial face; a medial (internal) visceral side applied to the lateral side of the trachea and the lower part of the larynx; and a posterior face moulded on the vascular-nervous bundle of the neck.

The isthmus is a flattened narrowing, higher than wide, with two faces (anterior and posterior) and two concave edges (top and bottom). From its upper edge, to the left of the median line, an inconstant extension of variable length stands out: the pyramidal lobe.

Aspect. The parenchyma is reddish brown and of soft consistency, enveloped by a fibrous capsule that adheres to it. The encapsulated gland lies within a cellular layer extending onto the vascular pedicles; it is through this sheath that the gland is mobilised in its lodge.

subject: subj:anat3

body.html:
1. Know the descriptive anatomy of the thyroid gland.
  2. Describe the anatomical relations of the thyroid gland.
  3. Name the pedicles that ensure the vascularization of the thyroid.
  4. Explain the physiology of the thyroid gland.
  5. Name the actions of thyroid hormones.

Thyroid hormones, secreted by the follicular cells:

  • Acceleration of enzymatic metabolism: increased oxygen consumption and heat production.
  • Acceleration of carbohydrate metabolism, leading to a decrease in blood sugar levels.
  • Acceleration of lipid catabolism.
  • Acceleration of diuresis.
  • Hypercalcemic action by accelerating bone resorption.
  • Action on cartilage ossification and growth.

Calcitonin, secreted by the C cells: a hypocalcemic hormone that inhibits bone demineralization, preventing the passage of calcium into the blood. It is regulated by the level of calcium in the blood.

Parathyroid secretion, discharged directly into the bloodstream through the capillary network of the connective tissue. It participates in the regulation of phosphocalcic metabolism with vitamin D and calcitonin. It is hypercalcemic, increasing bone resorption and promoting intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption of calcium, and hypophosphoremic, decreasing renal reabsorption of phosphates.

The gland is covered by two capsules:

  1. True capsule: formed by peripheral condensation of the fibrous stroma of the gland.
  2. False capsule: derived from splitting of the pretracheal fascia. Through it the gland is attached to the oblique lines of the thyroid cartilage and to the body of the hyoid bone in the midline. On the medial surface of the lobe it thickens to form the suspensory ligament of Berry, connecting the lobe to the cricoid cartilage.

The dense venous plexus lies deep to the true capsule, unlike that of the prostate gland. To avoid haemorrhage during thyroidectomy, the gland is removed along with the true capsule.

There is a cleavage or dissection plane between the thyroid body and its lodge: the thyroid space.

The cervical wall in front of the gland, from surface to depth: the skin and adipose pannicle; the fascia superficialis, which laterally envelops the platysma of the neck; the subcutaneous tissue; the superficial layer of the cervical fascia, covering the sternocleidomastoid muscles laterally and containing the anterior jugular veins; and the pretracheal blade of the cervical fascia, made of two sheets enclosing the subhyoid muscles.

The medial edges of the sternocleidohyoid and sternothyroid muscles limit the tracheostomy landmarks. At the level of this diamond-shaped area lies the white line of the neck.

With the laryngo-tracheal axis

The posterior aspect of the isthmus covers the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings, attached to the trachea by the thyro-tracheal ligament, the median ligament of Berry.

The inner side of the lateral lobes, forward, covers from top to bottom the posteroinferior part of the thyroid cartilage, the lateral surface of the cricoid cartilage, and the lateral face of the first five or six tracheal rings. The posteromedial border is attached to the first three tracheal rings by the thyro-tracheal ligament (the medial lateral ligament of Berry). The thyroid body is therefore united with the trachea and the larynx, and follows their movement during swallowing. Backwards, the medial side responds to the pharynx and then to the oesophagus.

Inferior laryngeal (recurrent) nerves

The recurrent nerve is the capital nerve for swallowing, phonation and protection of the airways. It has a very intimate relationship with the thyroid tissue, shows anatomical variations, differs between the two sides, and is at risk of injury in thyroid surgery.

SideCourse
RightOriginates from the pneumogastric at the level of the right subclavian artery, gradually approaches the right oesophageal angle, passes in front of the branches of the inferior thyroid artery, then under the fibres of the inferior constrictor muscle of the pharynx
LeftArises from the pneumogastric below the aortic arch, has a mediastinal course between the trachea and the aortic arch, runs along the oesotracheal angle in front of the left edge of the oesophagus, passes behind the branches of the inferior thyroid artery and the left inferior parathyroid, then under the fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor

Parathyroid glands

Two small endocrine glands on each side, orange-yellow in colour and flattened, located in the fat of the thyroid space, with anatomical and functional importance and a specific pathology. The inferior parathyroid lies on the posteromedial border of the lateral lobe, outside the inferior laryngeal nerve, below the termination of the inferior thyroid artery. The superior parathyroid lies on the same posteromedial border.

The thyroid is located in the infrahyoid region, in front of the upper end of the trachea and the lower part of the larynx, just behind the infrahyoid muscles. It lies in the lower part of the front and side of the neck opposite C5, C6, C7 and T1, clasping the upper part of the trachea.

MuscleAttachments
ThyrohyoidSuperiorly to the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone; inferiorly to the body of the thyroid cartilage
SternothyroidSuperiorly to the thyroid cartilage; inferiorly to the back of the manubrium and first costal cartilage. It lies deep to sternohyoid
SternohyoidSuperiorly to the body of the hyoid; inferiorly to the manubrium sterni and adjacent clavicle
OmohyoidSuperior and inferior bellies united by an intermediate tendon. Superiorly to the body of the hyoid; inferiorly to the lateral end of the superior border of the scapula by the suprascapular notch

These four pairs of strap muscles are enclosed in a fascial sheath in the anterior neck. They fix or depress the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech, and are supplied by the anterior rami of the upper three cervical nerves.

The superior thyroid pedicle is the only true pedicle of each lobe, approaching the superior pole and made of the superior thyroid artery and veins. The inferior thyroid artery reaches the posteromedial border above the base and divides into three branches. The middle thyroid veins arise from the posterolateral border and drain into the internal jugular vein. The inferior thyroid veins are not satellite to the artery; they form at the inferior border of the isthmus and the base of the lateral lobe.

VesselOrigin and branches
Superior thyroid arteryThe first branch of the external carotid artery. Ends at the top of the lateral lobe, dividing into a lateral branch, a medial (internal) branch joining the upper border of the isthmus and anastomosing with its contralateral counterpart, and a posterior branch
Inferior thyroid arteryA branch of the thyrocervical trunk, a collateral of the subclavian artery. Divides into a posterior branch ascending on the posterior aspect of the lobe and anastomosing with its counterpart from the superior thyroid artery, an inferior branch anastomosing with its contralateral counterpart along the inferior border of the isthmus, and a middle branch
Superior thyroid veinFrom the upper pole, accompanying the artery, into the internal jugular vein, most often via the thyro-linguo-facial (Farabeuf) trunk
Middle thyroid veinsFrom the lateral lobe, directly into the internal jugular vein
Inferior thyroid veinsFrom the inferior border of the isthmus and the base of the lateral lobe, descending to the left brachiocephalic vein

Lymphatics. From a fine subcapsular network arise the median collectors, going to either the prelaryngeal or the pretracheal nodes, and the lateral collectors, which subdivide into pedicles going to the jugular nodes.

The brain is hollow. Inside it is a connected set of cavities, the ventricles, filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The same fluid also surrounds the brain and spinal cord in the subarachnoid space.

Learn it as a one-way pipe: made by the choroid plexus, flows lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Magendie and Luschka → subarachnoid space, and is absorbed by the arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses. Block the pipe anywhere and the ventricles upstream swell: hydrocephalus.

body.html:
• Describe the anatomy and location of the cerebral ventricles.
  • Identify the main landmarks (walls) of each ventricle.
  • Explain how the ventricles connect with the subarachnoid space.
  • Describe CSF production, circulation, absorption and functions.
  • Explain the basic mechanisms of hydrocephalus and its consequences.
  • Recognise the anatomy behind lumbar puncture and ventricular drainage.

Four ventricles in a communicating network inside the brain parenchyma: 2 lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, the cerebral aqueduct and the fourth ventricle.

Embryology: the cavity of the neural tube becomes the ventricles as the brain vesicles form. By the sixth week:

Brain vesicleCavity
Cerebral hemispheresLateral ventricles
DiencephalonThird ventricle (joined to the lateral ventricles by the foramina of Monro)
Mesencephalon (midbrain)Cerebral aqueduct, which stays a narrow channel
HindbrainFourth ventricle

Paired, C-shaped CSF spaces in the cerebral hemispheres, each joined to the third ventricle by the interventricular foramen of Monro. Each has three horns (frontal, temporal, occipital), a body and an atrium where they meet.

PartRoofFloorMedial wallLateral wall
Frontal (anterior) horn: in the frontal lobe, in front of the foramen of MonroGenu of the corpus callosum (also the anterior wall)Rostrum of the corpus callosumSeptum pellucidum; columns of the fornix belowHead of the caudate nucleus
Body: from the foramen of Monro back to the atriumBody of the corpus callosumThalamusSeptum pellucidum (above) and body of the fornix (below)Caudate nucleus and thalamus
Atrium: triangular, joins body, temporal and occipital hornsBody and splenium of the corpus callosum; tapetumCollateral trigone (continuation of the collateral eminence)Calcar avis (from the calcarine fissure) and bulb of the corpus callosum (forceps major)Tapetum
Temporal (inferior) horn: the longest and largest; ends at the amygdalaThalamus, tail of the caudate, tapetumCollateral eminence and hippocampusChoroidal fissure runs along itTapetum (separates it from the optic radiations)
Occipital (posterior) horn: curves back from the atrium; size variesTapetumCollateral trigoneBulb of the corpus callosum and calcar avisTapetum (separates it from the optic radiations)

The tapetum is a sheet of crossing fibres from the splenium of the corpus callosum. The striothalamic sulcus separates the caudate tail from the thalamus.

A median cleft between the two thalami. It opens into the lateral ventricles by the foramina of Monro and into the fourth ventricle by the aqueduct of Sylvius, just below the posterior commissure. Choroid plexus lies along its roof.

WallFormed by
Lateral wallsThalami; the hypothalamic sulcus separates them from the hypothalamus (in front) and subthalamus (behind)
Anterior wall (top to bottom)Columns of the fornix, anterior commissure, lamina terminalis
Posterior wall (top to bottom)Habenular commissure, pineal gland, posterior commissure
RoofChoroidal fissure and bodies of the fornix
Floor (front to back)Optic chiasm, infundibulum of the pituitary, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies

The tuber cinereum is the part of the hypothalamus in the floor between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies.

Cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius): a narrow channel through the midbrain, joining the third to the fourth ventricle. It normally has no choroid plexus and is a common site of obstruction in non-communicating hydrocephalus.

Fourth ventricle: a broad, tent-shaped cavity behind the brainstem and in front of the cerebellum.

  • Roof (dorsal): superior and inferior medullary vela, over the cerebellum. Choroid plexus lies along the roof on the tela choroidea and can protrude through the foramina of Luschka.
  • Floor (ventral): the rhomboid fossa, a diamond-shaped depression on the back of the pons and upper half of the medulla.
  • Side walls: the vela and the cerebellar peduncles.
  • Obex: the most caudal tip.

Floor landmarks: the median sulcus divides the floor into right and left halves; the sulcus limitans divides each half. Motor nuclei lie medial to the sulcus limitans (the medial eminence); sensory nuclei lie lateral (the vestibular area).

Exits: CSF enters from the aqueduct and leaves through the median aperture of Magendie into the cisterna magna, the two lateral apertures of Luschka into the cerebellopontine cisterns, or down through the obex into the central canal of the spinal cord.

• A network of capillaries lined by specialised (ependymal) cells.
  • Lines all the ventricles except the frontal and occipital horns of the lateral ventricles and the cerebral aqueduct.
  • The main source of CSF, about 500 mL a day.
  • Forms the blood-CSF barrier.

LayerKey facts
Dura mater (outer, against the skull)Tough, fibrous, does not stretch. Divides the cranial cavity with the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. The dural venous sinuses lie between its two layers and drain into the internal jugular veins.
Arachnoid mater (middle)Avascular. Its projections into the dura, the arachnoid granulations (of Pacchioni), return CSF to the venous sinuses.
Pia mater (inner)Very thin, stuck to the brain and cord; the only layer that follows the gyri and fissures.

Spaces: epidural (skull to dura), subdural (dura to arachnoid), subarachnoid (arachnoid to pia, filled with CSF).

Cisterns are places where the subarachnoid space widens. They are connected, so keeping them open is essential for CSF flow, and some carry vessels and cranial nerves. Lecture list: cisterna magna, Sylvian, cerebellomedullary, lamina terminalis, velum interpositum, suprasellar (chiasmatic), carotid, perimesencephalic, superior cerebellar, prepontine, cerebellopontine and premedullary cisterns.

Lecture values
NatureClear, colourless ultrafiltrate of plasma; low in protein; few white cells; contains glucose and electrolytes
VolumeAbout 150 mL in the adult: 125 mL in the subarachnoid spaces, 25 mL in the ventricles
Production400 to 600 mL a day (about 500), mostly by the choroid plexus; renewed several times a day (the lecture says 4 to 5 times in 24 hours)
FlowOne way, rostral to caudal: lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle → Magendie (and Luschka) → subarachnoid space at the base of the brain
AbsorptionArachnoid villi and granulations into the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus, and around spinal nerve roots. Meningeal lymphatics and perivascular routes also help.

Functions: mechanical protection (cushion), buoyancy (lowers the brain's effective weight), chemical stability (removes waste, keeps homeostasis) and carrying nutrients and neuroactive substances. Slower CSF turnover may help metabolites build up in ageing and neurodegeneration. Because its composition is tightly controlled, changes in it help diagnosis.

Hydrocephalus is abnormal enlargement of the ventricles from disturbed CSF dynamics. Mechanisms: obstruction of flow, impaired absorption and, rarely, overproduction (for example a choroid plexus papilloma).

TypeCause
CommunicatingPoor absorption, or too much CSF produced; the pathway is open
Non-communicating (obstructive)Flow blocked in a passage between ventricles, often the aqueduct

Treatment: a shunt that drains CSF elsewhere, usually the peritoneal cavity (ventriculoperitoneal shunt), or endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), which opens the floor of the third ventricle so CSF reaches the interpeduncular cistern and bypasses a block below.

Other conditions: a mass raising intracranial pressure effaces the cisterns; subarachnoid haemorrhage fills cisterns with blood; meningitis infects the meninges and CSF.

Lumbar puncture: the cord ends at about L1-L2 in adults but the lumbar subarachnoid space continues below it, so the needle goes in at L3-L4 or L4-L5.
